This matters for Seminar XI because Lacan opens by asking what authorises him to speak. Once deprived of the institutional authority of recognised training status, what remains as the basis of analytic authority? Fink hears the questions "What is psychoanalysis?" and "Is psychoanalysis a science?" as inseparable from that institutional crisis.

Scientificity can easily become the language in which an institution expels an opponent. To call someone's work unscientific is to invoke an authority seemingly higher than political conflict. Fink therefore treats Lacan's analysis of science as partly an inquiry into what forms of authority can legitimately ground psychoanalysis.

### Psychoanalysis between science and religion

Fink reads the beginning of Seminar XI as setting up an apparent opposition between science and religion, only to displace psychoanalysis from both. Lacan suggests that psychoanalysis may be able to illuminate what counts as science and religion from a position not simply contained in either.

The first distinction concerns **research**. Lacan is suspicious of the ideal of the researcher who seeks truth, invoking Picasso's statement, "I do not seek, I find." Fink contrasts this with the religious formula that one would not seek if one had not already found. In religion and in hermeneutically oriented human sciences, the act of seeking can become endless. Meaning generates more meaning without an intrinsic stopping point.

Paul Ricoeur serves as Fink's principal example of a hermeneutic reading of psychoanalysis. In such an approach interpretation is indefinitely extendable. There is no terminal reference to truth and no point at which interpretation must answer to something other than further interpretation.

Fink argues that Lacanian psychoanalysis rejects this model. Interpretation aims at **truth** and may be said to create truth by producing a new symbolic articulation that touches the real. In this respect psychoanalysis resembles what Lacan values in genuine scientific invention: not the endless commentary on already available meaning, but the production of a new formalisation.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 69 | PRINTED PAGE 58]

### Why psychoanalysis is nevertheless not simply a science

Fink traces changes in Lacan's position. The early Lacan, including the doctoral work of the 1930s, could speak as if psychological phenomena would eventually yield to increasingly refined scientific analysis. This was not Freud's biological determinism, but it remained a form of confidence in scientific determinacy.

By 1964 Lacan can place psychoanalysis among the **conjectural sciences**, with game theory as an important comparison. A game-theoretical subject is stripped of personal substance and defined by a position inside a symbolic matrix of possible moves. Such a model is attractive because it formalises decision and probability without needing a psychological portrait of the player.

Fink nevertheless argues that the position shifts again in "Science and Truth." Modern science becomes a historical **precondition** for psychoanalysis rather than the class to which psychoanalysis belongs. Psychoanalysis is made possible by scientific discourse but is not itself one more scientific discipline among linguistics, anthropology and physics.

This distinction is especially important in what Fink calls the American empiricist context. Lacan does not equate science with the accumulation of observable facts. Fink places him in the history-of-science tradition represented by Alexandre Koyre, Georges Canguilhem and debates around logical positivism, Thomas Kuhn, Imre Lakatos and Paul Feyerabend. Scientific fields are constituted through concepts, symbolic frameworks and theoretical ruptures, not merely induced from raw data.

Structural linguistics and anthropology initially seemed to offer Lacan models for a new kind of scientific psychoanalysis because they formalised relations rather than psychologising individuals. But Fink says Lacan later becomes dissatisfied even with that analogy. Psychoanalysis begins to claim the capacity to judge the exclusions and limitations of established sciences rather than asking those sciences to certify it.

### Descartes and the scientific exclusion of truth

Fink locates the key divergence in the relation to **truth**. His Lacanian reading of Descartes is historical rather than narrowly philosophical. Descartes searches for certainty and ultimately finds it in the cogito. Questions of eternal or mathematical truth are guaranteed by God and are thereby displaced from the human knower.

Fink presents this move as liberating modern science from the burden of transcendental truth. Scientific discourse can develop internally coherent symbolic grids, laws and mathematical relations without continuously grounding them in Scripture, metaphysics or a theory of ultimate truth. Knowledge acquires its own momentum.

Formal logic illustrates the result.

[FIGURE / TABLE: Truth values in propositional logic]
Source location: PDF page 72, printed page 61.
Description: A standard truth table shows combinations of propositions and assigns `T` or `F` to the compound statement. Fink's point is that "true" and "false" here operate as formal values inside an axiomatic system, comparable to binary values such as `1/0`, rather than as philosophical claims about transcendent truth.
Transcription status: conceptual reconstruction; the exact table is routine and is not reproduced line-for-line.

Modern science can therefore employ truth values while excluding the broader question of truth. Fink's thesis is that psychoanalysis assumes precisely this abandoned burden. The analytic field cannot be satisfied with internally correct symbolic relations if it ignores the truth that speaks through symptoms, slips, fantasy and desire.

### Psychologization of the subject

Fink then explains Lacan's polemic against the **psychologization of the subject**. Lucien Levy-Bruhl provides the negative example: so-called primitive peoples are explained through attributed beliefs and feelings and are positioned on a developmental ladder below modern Western rationality.

Claude Levi-Strauss is closer to Lacan's scientific ideal because he analyses symbolic distinctions, kinship rules and structural oppositions rather than trying to enter informants' conscious psychology. Fink nevertheless notes that Lacan remains critical even of structural anthropology insofar as it also leaves truth outside its field.

Psychologization means taking conscious attitudes as explanatory causes. Fink extends the criticism to everyday explanations that derive collective action from what people supposedly feel about empire, nation or fatherland. Freud's unconscious already makes such accounts inadequate. Lacan radicalises the point by treating the unconscious as the **discourse of the Other**: inherited phrases, commands, prohibitions, conventions and signifying structures from family and culture become constitutive of the subject.

The same criticism is directed at developmental models that treat children or non-Western peoples as incomplete versions of the normal adult. Fink calls this, following Levi-Strauss, the **archaic illusion**. A more rigorous approach reconstructs the synchronic system and its transformations on its own terms rather than measuring it by a pre-given norm.

### The conjectural sciences and positional subjects

Game theory allows Fink to clarify how far formalisation can go. A player can be reduced to a position, a finite set of legal moves and a defined goal. Probabilities and optimal moves can then be calculated without a psychology of the individual player.

Lacan's category of conjectural science also undermines a crude opposition between exact and human sciences. Quantum mechanics itself relies on probabilities. If physics can be probabilistic while remaining exact, formalised conjecture is not automatically non-scientific.

Yet Fink insists that psychoanalysis cannot finally reduce its subject to a calculable position with a simple aim. That would repeat structuralism's tendency to let the combinatory run without subject or object.

### Subject and cause

The decisive remainder is **cause**. Fink recalls Lacan's argument from Seminar X that scientific progress tends to erase cause by closing the gap between cause and effect with increasingly comprehensive laws. When everything follows smoothly from structure, "cause" becomes merely shorthand for a lawful sequence.

Lacan wants a stronger notion: cause as what interrupts the lawlike chain, what remains inexplicable from the standpoint of available knowledge. Science assumes that any such remainder will eventually be incorporated into law. Psychoanalysis retains the remainder as structurally significant.

Fink therefore distinguishes two faces of the subject:

1. the **pure subject** of the combinatory, defined entirely by a position in the symbolic structure;
2. the **saturated subject**, Lacan's term for the subject in a libidinal relation to an object of jouissance.

The second subject cannot be understood without object `a` as cause of desire. The fantasy formula, conventionally `$ ◊ a`, writes a relation between the barred subject and this cause. Alienation gives the subject's dependence on signifiers; separation brings in the libidinal object that prevents structure from being the whole story.

Psychoanalysis therefore keeps open two concepts modern science finds troublesome: **subject** and **cause**. Fink closes with Lacan's provocative suggestion that if object `a` as cause were genuinely introduced into scientific discourse, science itself would be transformed.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Institutional certification versus analytic authority.
- Science, religion and psychoanalysis.
- Finding versus endless hermeneutic seeking.
- Truth-producing interpretation versus unbounded meaning.
- Modern science as precondition for psychoanalysis, not identical with it.
- Empiricism versus conceptual construction of scientific fields.
- Scientific knowledge versus the excluded burden of truth.
- Psychologization versus symbolic determination.
- Conjectural sciences and positional subjects.
- Structure versus cause as rupture.
- Pure subject versus saturated/libidinal subject.
- Object `a` as cause of desire.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Fink reads Seminar XI's opening epistemological questions as inseparable from Lacan's institutional excommunication. The seminar asks whether psychoanalysis can ground its authority through something other than recognised institutional certification or a borrowed scientific status. Its eventual answer lies in a distinct relation to truth, subject, cause and jouissance.

### Interpretive status

The essay is Fink's synthesis of Seminar XI with "Position of the Unconscious," "Science and Truth," Seminar X and later Lacanian formalisation. His conclusion that psychoanalysis is not itself a science under Lacanian criteria is explicitly presented as his reading of Lacan's evolving position.

### Sources used

- Bruce Fink, "Science and Psychoanalysis," *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 66-75, printed pages 55-64.


## Francois Regnault - The Name-of-the-Father

**Author:** Francois Regnault  
**Source location:** PDF pages 76-85; printed pages 65-74

### Governing question and thesis

Regnault begins with a deliberately simple question: if fatherhood is central to psychoanalysis, why does Lacan insist on the **Name-of-the-Father**? His answer follows the concept from the symbolic father, through paternal metaphor and foreclosure, toward topology and the later Borromean pluralisation of the Names-of-the-Father. Across those transformations the invariant is **naming as substitution**. Fatherhood in the analytic sense is not first a natural or biological relation but a signifying function that supports law, separation and orientation in the symbolic order.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 76 | PRINTED PAGE 65]

### A major Lacanian concept that is not one of the four fundamentals

Regnault insists on a distinction of status. The Name-of-the-Father is crucial to Lacan, but it is not one of the four concepts Lacan calls fundamental in Seminar XI. Its importance is signalled instead by the seminar Lacan had planned for 1963 and abandoned after institutional exclusion. Lacan never returned to the project under exactly the same title, though the problem proliferates throughout later teaching.

Regnault takes the 1973-1974 title *Les non-dupes errent* as an example. The phrase is homophonically equivalent in French to *Les Noms-du-Pere*. The substitution itself is theoretically meaningful: the father's name can be displaced by another signifying chain. The nature of the name is precisely to substitute.

### The symbolic father versus the empirical father

Regnault returns to the Rome discourse to establish the starting point. The father supports the symbolic order and the law. Lacan's structural move is to distinguish the **symbolic function of the father** from the child's imaginary identifications with a particular father and from the empirical acts of the biological man.

This is why Regnault says that the father is first a name or signifier and only secondarily a person. Biological procreation does not by itself constitute psychoanalytic fatherhood. Animals have progenitors, but, strictly speaking, they do not have fathers, mothers, uncles or cousins except insofar as humans insert them into symbolic genealogies such as pedigrees.

Clinically, the child first encounters maternal desire. But beyond that desire the child can encounter a law to which the mother herself refers or submits. The paternal function does not simply place a man beside mother and child. It inserts a signifying reference that prevents the mother-child relation from being treated as self-sufficient.

Regnault therefore describes separation not simply as separation of child from mother but as a transformation in the status of the breast or other cause of desire. The maternal object and the symbolic law become distinguishable.

### Name, debt, genealogy and religion

The Name-of-the-Father raises a double problem: father as name, and proper name as transmitted through the father. "Father" is not simply a Russellian proper name, yet the child often receives a family name through paternal genealogy. The symbolic debt attached to paternity participates in the circulation of objects, goods and marriage relations inside kinship systems.

Regnault notes that Freud already approached paternity as symbolic. *Totem and Taboo* shows kinship terms operating beyond empirical procreation. Freud also ties fatherhood to the **dead father**. Regnault nevertheless argues that Lacan radicalises the point by treating the recognition of paternity as the effect of a **pure signifier**.

Religion is central to this history. Lacan's examples show that paternity can be symbolically attributed even when biological causation is irrelevant or unknown. Regnault therefore says that the concept of the Name-of-the-Father comes as much from religion as from science. Christianity makes the Father's name explicit at the highest theological level, though Regnault also notes that religions do not form a homogeneous class and that, for example, the Koran refuses Christian divine paternity.

The grammatical construction "Name-of-the-Father" itself remains productive. It can be heard as the names by which the Father is called, or as the names the Father gives. The ambiguity is not to be resolved because it belongs to the structure of naming.

### The paternal metaphor

Naming becomes technically precise through metaphor. Regnault states that the Name-of-the-Father is a metaphor because one signifier is substituted for another. The crucial substitution concerns the place of the mother's desire and produces phallic signification.

[FORMULA / MATHEME: General formula of metaphor]
Source location: PDF page 80, printed page 69.
Visual structure: A signifier is substituted for another signifier in a fractional arrangement; the operation yields a new signified. The source glosses `S` as signifier, `x` as unknown signification, and `s` as the produced signified.
Authorial function: To show that metaphor is a formal operation of substitution rather than a poetic resemblance.
Transcription status: visually verified; exact typographic spacing is not reproduced because the HTML-derived source uses damaged custom glyphs.

[FORMULA / MATHEME: Paternal metaphor]
Source location: PDF page 80, printed page 69.
Visual structure: `Name-of-the-Father / Desire of the Mother` is placed in a substitution relation to `Desire of the Mother / Signified to the subject`, producing `Name-of-the-Father` and a phallic signification in the field of the Other.
Authorial function: The paternal name occupies the place opened by maternal absence/desire and produces the signification of the phallus.
Transcription status: descriptive reconstruction from the rendered page.

The *fort-da* game provides Regnault with the model of absence that can be named. A signifier appears in the place of maternal absence, and through this substitution the child's relation to desire becomes organised symbolically.

### Foreclosure and psychosis

When this signifier is not available to perform its function, Lacan speaks of **foreclosure of the Name-of-the-Father**. Regnault describes foreclosure as exclusion or elimination from the symbolic battery, not simply repression of an already present representation.

The Name-of-the-Father is peculiar because its signification concerns the missing signifier itself. Regnault links the operation to Schreber: the crisis around being unable to become a father is followed by the delusional transformation through which Schreber becomes God's wife. The paternal place returns in the real in another form once it cannot function in the expected symbolic way.

Regnault also draws on "Position of the Unconscious," where the paternal metaphor appears as a **principle of separation** within the Other. Kinship, ideals and paternal metaphor contribute to the institutions and norms by which subjects receive prescriptions concerning what men and women are to do. This does not amount to a natural definition of sex; the norms are signifying constructions in the field of the Other.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 81 | PRINTED PAGE 70]

### Schema R and the paternal function

Regnault then traces the Name-of-the-Father through Lacan's Schema R.

[FIGURE: Schema R]
Source location: PDF page 81, printed page 70.
Description: A square/quadrangular schema combining symbolic and imaginary triangles with a central quadrangle labelled `R`. Visible labels include `S`, `I`, `M`, `F`, imaginary terms `i/m`, and positions associated with ego and Other. `F` marks the Name-of-the-Father in the Other.
Authorial function: To display the relations among symbolic, imaginary and real and to show the paternal function as an orienting position in the subject's structure.
Transcription status: visually verified descriptive reconstruction.

Regnault gives both static and historical readings. The imaginary triangle concerns narcissistic relations and ego formation. The symbolic triangle includes ego ideal, mother/primal object and the Name-of-the-Father. The real appears as a remainder produced by the symbolic's effect on the imaginary. Historically, the scheme can also be read from relation to the mother through ego images toward paternal identification.

### Topological transformation: the subject as cut and object as remnant

Regnault stresses that Lacan later reinterprets Schema R topologically rather than only geometrically.

[FIGURE: Schema R topologically transformed]
Source location: PDF page 82, printed page 71.
Description: A series of drawings converts the flat Schema R into a unilateral/Moebius-like surface by identifying edges such as `i` with `I` and `m` with `M`.
Authorial function: The subject becomes the cut made in the surface, while the object is what falls away as a remnant produced by that cut. Interpretation is the operation that cuts and thereby produces both subject and object.
Transcription status: visually verified descriptive reconstruction.

The conceptual effect is important. The subject is not an entity sitting somewhere on the surface; it has the structure of an **edge or cut**. Object `a` is not a substantive object represented inside the scheme; it has the structure of a **fallen remainder**. Interpretation makes these structures appear by cutting.

### From fixed point to Borromean knot

In the earlier flat schema the Name-of-the-Father can appear as a fixed orienting point. Regnault then moves to the later Borromean topology, where the problem changes from locating a point to understanding how real, symbolic and imaginary hold together.

[FIGURE: Borromean knot of Real, Imaginary and Symbolic]
Source location: PDF page 83, printed page 72.
Description: Three interlinked rings labelled `R`, `I`, and `S`; a central region is associated with meaning. The rings are linked Borromean-wise so that removing one releases the other two.
Authorial function: To formalise the dependence of the three registers on a knotting relation rather than on bilateral pairings.
Transcription status: visually verified.

Regnault explicitly rejects treating this merely as an illustrative metaphor. Knotting and unknotting are presented as attempts to formalise the real structure of signifying linkage. He connects the analytic act of unknotting a symptom to this topological language.

The **joint** that holds the structure together is then identified with the Name-of-the-Father. But the late formula is more radical: the Name-of-the-Father is not simply one term inside the knot; it can be the **knot itself**.

### Name as hole, plural Names-of-the-Father, and the fourth term

Regnault's late Lacan brings the logic of naming to its limit. A proper name is placed over an absence. The thing itself has no final name; the name marks a hole while organising what can be said around it.

This leads Lacan to pluralise the concept. There are **Names-of-the-Father**. Real, symbolic and imaginary can themselves function as names insofar as they name something. The paternal function is no longer reducible to a single signifier with one theological or familial content.

Regnault also notes Lacan's move toward a fourth element. If it is impossible to determine uniquely which of the three consistencies should be privileged as "the real one," a fourth knotting term can support their linkage. The Name-of-the-Father can therefore appear as something added that secures the consistency of the symbolic and of the knot as a whole.

This movement anticipates the topological problems taken much further in Lacan's later teaching, but Regnault's purpose here is historical: to show how a concept that begins as a symbolic paternal signifier gradually becomes a general principle of naming and structural knotting.

### Three kinds of naming and the conclusion

Regnault closes by distinguishing symbolic, imaginary and real modes of naming. Symbolic naming inserts an element into the differential signifying order. Imaginary naming assumes a fit between name and thing. Naming of the real concerns the referent or, clinically, an encounter such as anxiety that resists signifying assimilation.

The Name-of-the-Father thus acquires ever more functions and eventually approaches **structure itself**. There can be many paternal names because no one proper name finally names the Father. Regnault reads this as the background to Lacan's strange but deliberate formulation that psychoanalysis brings the Name-of-the-Father back into scientific examination.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Symbolic father versus empirical/imaginary father.
- Father as signifier rather than biological procreator.
- Name given by the father versus name of the father.
- Religion and pure symbolic paternity.
- Naming as substitution.
- Paternal metaphor and phallic signification.
- Foreclosure of the Name-of-the-Father in psychosis.
- Paternal metaphor as principle of separation.
- Schema R and its topological reinterpretation.
- Subject as cut and object as remnant.
- Name-of-the-Father as fixed point, knot, hole and plural naming function.
- Borromean relation of Real, Imaginary and Symbolic.
- Possible fourth term supporting the three consistencies.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Although the essay ranges widely across Lacan's teaching, Regnault connects the Name-of-the-Father to Seminar XI through separation, the field of the Other and the changing status of the subject/object relation. The seminar's institutional background around the undelivered Names-of-the-Father project also gives the concept a special historical resonance.

### Interpretive status

This is explicitly a diachronic reconstruction by Regnault. The movement from the Rome discourse through paternal metaphor, Schema R and the Borromean knot combines texts from widely separated periods. The late topological account should not be retroactively treated as if it were already fully present in Seminar XI.

### Sources used

- Francois Regnault, "The Name-of-the-Father," *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 76-85, printed pages 65-74.


# Part III - Transference and the Drives

## Pierre-Gilles Gueguen - Transference as Deception

**Author:** Pierre-Gilles Gueguen  
**Source location:** PDF pages 87-100; printed pages 77-90

### Governing question and thesis

Gueguen treats transference as a practical problem of analytic technique and asks why a phenomenon apparently founded on error, passion and false attribution is nevertheless indispensable to psychoanalysis. His thesis is deliberately paradoxical: **transference deceives, but the deception is not an accidental contamination of treatment. It is one of the privileged ways in which truth, unconscious knowledge and the subject's relation to the object emerge.** The analyst therefore neither abolishes transference nor validates its apparent content. The task is to handle the transferential situation so that the analysand can work through the structure of the deception.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 87 | PRINTED PAGE 77]

### Transference in ordinary life: belief, passion and distorted transmission

Gueguen starts outside the consulting room. In ordinary human relations, transferential phenomena appear as love, hate, indifference, confidence, mistrust and anxiety. They obstruct the ideal of transparent communication. Politicians, educators, doctors and analysts all have to contend with unpredictable responses from those who address them. The more modern communication aspires to direct transmission, the more evident misunderstanding becomes.

He groups the relevant interference around Lacan's three passions: **love, hate and ignorance**. From a rationalist or scientific standpoint, transference looks like an insult to reason because affect distorts a message. Descartes' separation of passions from thought supplies one historical version of this ideal. But Gueguen immediately complicates the rationalist picture. Political, pedagogical, medical and analytic choices all require adherence, risk and belief. To choose an analyst is already to wager on someone as a legitimate representative of knowledge. No choice is wholly insulated from love or transference.

The first problem is therefore not simply how to eliminate deception but how a subject can act when every appeal to another person involves a risk of being duped. Gueguen places psychoanalysis alongside philosophical questions of certainty in Descartes, Kant and Wittgenstein, but insists that psychoanalysis does not solve uncertainty through a metalanguage capable of fixing all meanings.

### Freud: facsimile, false connection and the analyst's implication

Gueguen reconstructs Freud's early theory from the Dora case. Transference consists in **new editions, facsimiles or displacements of older impulses and fantasies** onto present persons, especially the analyst. The core idea is the *false connection*: something genuine is displaced and attributed elsewhere.

Lacan's linguistic rereading matters because the false connection can be understood as a displacement and substitution among signifiers, not merely as an affect attached to the wrong person. Gueguen thus reads Freud and Lacan together at this point: transference carries a movement from one signifier or signification to another before it is theorized as a stable two-person relationship.

Freud also sees the analyst as dependent on the patient's transference. In the introductory lectures transference is both the greatest danger to treatment and one of its most useful tools; in *The Question of Lay Analysis* it can become the true object of analytic work. The patient is deceived and the analyst can be lured, yet the illusion is precisely what analysis can interpret.

### Dora and subjective rectification

Dora provides Gueguen with a model of how analytic work differs from factual correction. Freud does not decide whether Dora has correctly judged her father's intentions. Instead he asks what part she has played in the situation she condemns. Lacan calls this movement **subjective rectification**.

The analyst therefore does not restore an objective past against a false present. What matters is how an imagined or remembered past is reenacted and constructed within current transference. In that sense analysand and analyst are both caught in the structure. A statement can be deceptive while still producing a truth effect.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 92 | PRINTED PAGE 82]

### 'You are telling the truth': deception, enunciation and interpretation

Gueguen turns directly to Seminar XI, where Lacan describes transference as a path of deceptiveness. This does not authorize the analyst to oppose deception by proclaiming the truth. Gueguen cites Lacan's formulation that, along the path where the subject errs, the analyst can be in the position of saying, in effect, **'You are telling the truth.'** Interpretation operates in that dimension.

The distinction between the **subject of the statement and the subject of enunciation** clarifies the point. A patient may try to persuade the analyst that he is fundamentally a good person, attempting to place the reassuring verdict in the Other's mouth. If the analyst refuses to occupy that position, the division the patient tried to transfer to the analyst returns to the patient. The truth at issue is not the factual opposite of the patient's statement. It is the truth of what the deceptive operation itself reveals about the divided subject.

### Love as motor and danger

Freud's later work allows Gueguen to sharpen the technical problem. A patient can continue on the path of deception because of love and may improve in order to win the analyst's approval. That makes transference a motor of treatment, but love can rapidly become hatred, and disappointed love can end treatment.

The analyst must therefore avoid both extremes. Excessive transferential love can create enchantment: patients dream for the analyst, try to become exemplary analysands and cease doing analytic work. Excessive hatred can lead to rupture. Gueguen describes handling transference as **countering its pressure without answering it with the analyst's own transference**. He invokes Colette Soler's phrase that the issue is not countertransference but how to counter transference, and uses the image of the 'pyromaniac fireman': fanning transference when insufficient and damping it when overwhelming.

This responsibility does not remove the analysand's responsibility. Lacan's reading of Dora implicates the subject in their own position. But once analysis has begun, the analyst assumes responsibility for the conditions under which transference develops and cannot simply abandon that responsibility when the situation becomes difficult.

### Power that must not be used

Gueguen links Freud's technical cautions to Lacan's *Direction of the Treatment*. Transference grants the analyst power, but that power provides a way out only on condition that it **not be used**. The analyst must not exploit dependency, frustrate the patient for its own sake, or take up the superego position.

This is part of Gueguen's distinction between transference and repetition. Repetition belongs to transference but does not exhaust it. What occurs in transference is not a shadow of an old scene merely reproduced in absentia. The analysand is subjected in the present to the analyst's desire and tries, among other things, to make the analyst love them. The deception is produced here and now, even when it carries the form of another scene.

This shifts the analytic question away from proving whether an early scene literally happened. The analyst works with the signifiers fixed in trauma and with the current structure in which the subject seeks the Other's response.

### Freud's limit and object a

Gueguen notes Freud's skepticism in *Analysis Terminable and Interminable* about passing beyond certain points associated with the Oedipus complex and castration. Lacan's invention of **object a** is presented as an attempt to go further, but not by discovering an ultimate historical truth. Object a is a construction concerning the subject's relation to the object and the false connection itself, not a recovered fact at the origin.

### Ego psychology: therapeutic alliance and the analyst as reality standard

Gueguen devotes substantial space to ego psychology because it reveals what is at stake in Lacan's alternative. The ego-psychological **working or therapeutic alliance** imagines an adult contract between the patient's ego and the analyst's ego. Treatment is supposed to preserve a reasonable sector of the patient that can cooperate with the analyst against neurotic distortions.

Gueguen sees two problems. First, the analyst becomes the standard of objective reality: the transferential interpretation easily becomes 'you are taking me for someone else, but I am not that person in reality.' Second, the concept of adaptation cannot say which social reality is normative when historical values change. The example of debates over adapting people to reality before or after the Vietnam War exposes the instability of the supposedly objective standard.

The deeper contradiction is structural. Ego psychology begins with a contract between autonomous partners while also holding that the patient repeats childish false connections with the analyst. It then gives priority to strategic handling of the relationship and to countertransference as the analyst's emotional response.

For Lacan, by contrast, the analytic relation cannot be grounded in reciprocal egos. If one were to speak of a contract, Gueguen suggests, it would be a relation among the subject, the real and the unconscious, while the analyst occupies a **semblance** rather than the position of an equal contracting ego.

### Klein: primitive object relations and the reparative ideal

Melanie Klein provides a different alternative. In 'The Origins of Transference' she roots transference in primitive relations of love and hate and insists on negative transference. Primitive images of parents are not literal reproductions of real people. Fantasy and real experience are already mixed in the earliest object relations.

Gueguen credits Klein with moving beyond the ego-psychological equation of reality and objectivity, but he argues that her model still differs decisively from Lacan's. Klein's field remains organized by the imaginary and by a reparative movement toward the **total object**. After the idealized object has been destroyed in fantasy, treatment tends toward restoration of a more realistic and tempered relation to it. Gueguen reads this as a pastoral ideal of reform, parallel in a different register to ego psychology's adaptation to reality.

Lacan's object a instead introduces the **real** as something not reducible to either objective reality or a repaired imaginary relation.

### The Lacanian solution: the analysand analyzes the transference

For Gueguen psychoanalysis cannot be a process of disillusionment in which the analyst reveals the correct view. The analyst is not the **Other of the Other** and does not possess the truth to be handed over. The analyst establishes conditions for a rectification of truth, while the analysand develops the variations of their own fantasy.

In doing so, the analysand discovers the ways they try to reduce the analyst to a counterpart or object. Gueguen defines fantasy in precisely this interpersonal form: it stages the way subjects reduce others to places in their own scenario. Hence Lacan can call the fundamental fantasies of neurotics 'perverse' without saying that neurotic subjects are clinically perverse.

At the end of the work the subject may construct the **fundamental fantasy** and recognize the object-position that has fixed their relation to the Other. Gueguen associates this with Lacan's crossing or traversing of fantasy. Interpretation is not the transfer of hidden knowledge from analyst to patient; truth is verified by its effects.

### Subject supposed to know and the end of transference

Gueguen's final step defines analytic transference as **love addressed to knowledge**. The analysand loves the analyst because the analyst is supposed to possess the key to unconscious knowledge. At the beginning of treatment the subject supposes a subject who knows the truth about truth and pursues the signification of the symptom.

That supposition is itself a productive deception. Lacan does not locate final certainty in a completed body of unconscious knowledge. Analysis must eventually put an end to the transference, and Gueguen links this to a changed apprehension of the subject's relation to object a.

The contrast with other schools is therefore a contrast in aims. Ego psychology and, differently, Kleinian analysis orient themselves toward restoration of a better relation to reality. Gueguen presents the Lacanian aim as enabling the subject to **catch a glimpse of the real**.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Transference as deception rather than transparent communication.
- Love, hate and ignorance as passions interfering with knowledge.
- Freud's facsimile and false-connection model.
- Signifier displacement as Lacan's rereading of false connection.
- Subjective rectification in the Dora case.
- Statement versus enunciation in transferential deception.
- Truth effects without an analyst occupying the position of truth-teller.
- Handling transference versus interpreting it as a two-person affective relation.
- Transference as more than repetition.
- Analyst's power as a power that must not be used.
- Critique of therapeutic alliance, adaptation and countertransference.
- Klein's primitive object relations and reparative total-object ideal.
- Object a and the real.
- Fundamental fantasy and its traversal.
- Subject supposed to know.
- End of transference as a transformation of the subject's relation to object a.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Gueguen relies especially on Seminar XI's separation of transference from repetition, its account of transference as a path of deception, the analyst's desire and the subject supposed to know. The essay turns those conceptual distinctions into questions of technique: what the analyst should not claim to know, how transferential love is neither indulged nor extinguished, and how the deception can be used without converting analysis into education or adaptation.

### Examples and references

- Freud's Dora case and Lacan's reading of subjective rectification.
- Freud's introductory lectures, *The Question of Lay Analysis*, *An Outline of Psychoanalysis*, and *Analysis Terminable and Interminable*.
- Lacan's 'Seminar on The Purloined Letter' and 'The Direction of the Treatment'.
- Ego psychology's therapeutic alliance.
- Melanie Klein's 'The Origins of Transference'.
- The social-historical problem of defining the reality to which a patient should adapt.

### Interpretive status

Gueguen presents a Lacanian polemic against ego psychology and a selective contrast with Klein while also rereading Freud as closer to Lacan than post-Freudian adaptations suggest. Claims about the superiority of the Lacanian explanation are Gueguen's interpretive position, not propositions made directly by Lacan in Seminar XI.

### Sources used

- Pierre-Gilles Gueguen, 'Transference as Deception,' *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 87-100, printed pages 77-90.


## Jean-Pierre Klotz - The Passionate Dimension of Transference

**Author:** Jean-Pierre Klotz  
**Source location:** PDF pages 101-107; printed pages 91-97

### Governing question and thesis

Klotz approaches transference through **passion**. Transference is classically a form of love, but love is its phenomenal effect rather than its complete concept. The clinical task is to ask what causes this passionate effect and how its emergence can be used in directing treatment. Klotz's central move is Lacanian: affect is not ignored but relocated in relation to the **signifier, knowledge, lack and the real of sex**. Love, hate and especially ignorance become ways in which the subject's relation to the Other and to knowledge appears.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 101 | PRINTED PAGE 91]

### Transference love as unavoidable obstacle

Klotz begins from a familiar analytic paradox. Transference love is an obstacle to analysis, but it is an obstacle produced by analysis itself and cannot be bypassed. Its appearance is therefore also a gauge of what is happening in the treatment. The analyst should not construct the concept of transference from the psychology of being passionately in love. Rather, the occurrence of love forces the analyst to question the structure that causes it.

Seminar XI is decisive because Lacan rejects ordinary formulations of transference as a simple interpersonal feeling. Love can mislead, but the misleading belongs to the dimension of truth. The analytic encounter with truth does not occur by eliminating the deception of love in advance.

### Passion as discontinuity: love, hate and ignorance

Klotz illustrates passion with three statements: a colleague's declaration that he is passionately fond of psychoanalysis; an analysand's complaint of being bored and fed up with analysis; and the statement, from analysand or analyst, that one understands nothing about psychoanalysis. All three interrupt ordinary discourse. They stand out as discontinuities that can have an awakening effect.

The third case shows why ignorance belongs with love and hate. Lacan treats **ignorance as a passion**, and transference is inseparable from knowledge. A declaration of not knowing is therefore not merely an absence of information. It can mark a passionate relation to a gap in knowledge.

### Freud, transference love and resistance

Klotz contrasts this with Freud's scientific ambition. Freud foregrounds sex and unconscious formations rather than a general theory of passion. Yet transference love emerges in clinical work as resistance: free association is interrupted and the analyst becomes the object of a passion generated by the treatment.

The goal of love is not the same as the goal of analytic work. The problem is therefore how to treat a passion that analysis itself produces. Klotz rejects the stereotype that Lacan neglects affect. Lacan's move is instead to understand affect through its relation to the signifier and the structure of the subject.

### The 'passion of the signifier'

The word *passion* carries a religious history in which suffering and passivity are followed by active transformation. Klotz uses that double grammar to illuminate Lacan's expression **the passion of the signifier**. The subject suffers the mark of the signifier, yet the signifier is also active: it determines effects of signification.

The signified is thus not an independent content subsequently labelled by words. It bears the mark of signifying action. In analytic terms, the patient is someone who suffers and is marked, but passion is not merely a contingent emotional quality of a pre-existing subject. It belongs structurally to the signifier that constitutes the subject.

This allows Klotz to connect the symbolic and affective without reducing one to the other.

### Desire, sex, phallus and lack

Klotz next relates passion to the broader Lacanian articulation of symbolic and real. Desire is the link. The real grounding analytic experience is sex, understood through the impossibility of fully symbolizing sexual relation. Hence the signifier's passion has to be considered together with the place, object and signifier of desire.

The **phallus** is privileged because Lacan introduces it as the signifier around which the subject's lack and sexual positioning are articulated. Klotz also invokes the later claim that love substitutes for a sexual relationship that does not exist. Passion therefore occupies the place where signification and sexual impossibility meet.

Any signifier can become passionate because signification is organized around lack. Klotz uses Lacan's rendering of *manque-a-etre* as **want-to-be** to stress the subject's simultaneous activity and submission. Passion manifests through demand, the form in which this want-to-be is addressed to the Other.

### Clinical case: phobia and the passion to know

Klotz's main example is a young woman with a severe animal phobia. She is an intellectually sophisticated, perpetual student with a pronounced passion for knowledge. Her relation to analysts is immediately structured by the question of sex: she challenges male analysts as men who cannot provide the answer a woman wants, even while continuing to demand such an answer. Klotz reads this as one manifestation of **woman as a question**.

Her father is associated with disappointment and with animals, including large dogs and a donkey. Relations with women are no easier. She regards being a woman as a curse and maintains what Klotz calls a hateful complicity with her mother. The entire family atmosphere acquires the repulsive quality attached to the feared animals.

Her employment history also turns on passion. She organizes choices according to whether something 'interests' her. Entry into analysis is experienced as a choice of freedom against the final restricting bond of the phobia. After transferential crises and a temporary interruption, she takes a stable managerial job for which she is highly qualified but toward which she feels no passion.

### From phobia to anxiety and the Other's gaze

A frightening feminine figure gradually emerges in fantasy as a witch, accompanied by fear that she may harm others, especially men. A promotion at work intensifies the problem. Recognition of her abilities is intolerable because she cannot identify what others see in her that warrants recognition.

Her discourse turns to transparency, envy and fear of finding herself. Klotz links this to the **Other's gaze**: what is opaque in the very place where she imagines herself transparent.

A crucial event concerns a spider, previously a powerful phobic object. It now produces only ordinary fear. But disappearance of the localized phobia is not uncomplicated improvement. Anxiety becomes generalized and is reorganized around the question of what she herself may be for the Other. Klotz formulates the dilemma as a forced choice: either endure the phobic object or regard herself as a filthy, dangerous animal capable of harming the Other.

The shift exposes the void around which the phobia had been constructed. The phobic animal had localized and helped the subject avoid a more fundamental gap.

### Knowledge, ignorance and symbolic castration

The woman's passion to know persists. Psychoanalytic knowledge becomes an object of intense curiosity, as is common in hysteria. Yet periods of intellectual activity are interrupted by staring into what appears to be a hole. Psychoanalysis increasingly becomes a point of **ignorance**, not a body of answers.

Klotz reads the movement from phobia to generalized anguish as the beginning of a different relation to knowledge. The gap in knowledge and the discontinuity it produces belong to **symbolic castration**. Passion covers over a separation between subject and Other, even though the subject only exists as an effect of that Other's signifying order.

The hysterical subject is particularly useful for showing this dynamic because hysteria actively addresses the Other. The obsessive more often seeks to avoid the Other and is, in Klotz's shorthand, closer to the passion of hate. This is why Lacan can speak of the necessary **hystericization** of the analysand: analysis must put the subject to work in relation to the Other and the question of knowledge.

Ignorance finally provides the most general name for the neurotic's passionate relation to knowledge. It is not simple lack of information but a structured way of not knowing.

### The unresolved question of the analyst's passion

Klotz returns at the end to the psychoanalyst who declared his passion for psychoanalysis. One might expect neurotic passion to diminish at the end of analysis, yet Lacan can also speak of a new or increased passion tied to the assumption of symbolic castration. Klotz leaves the essay on a productive question: **when an analysand becomes an analyst, what becomes of passion?** The problem of the analyst's desire is thus approached through a transformation rather than simple extinction of passionate investment.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Transference as love versus transference as a concept.
- Passion as discontinuity in analytic discourse.
- Love, hate and ignorance as passions.
- Knowledge and ignorance in transference.
- Affect relocated through the signifier rather than denied.
- Passion of the signifier.
- *Manque-a-etre* / want-to-be.
- Desire as link between symbolic and real.
- Phallus and the impossibility of sexual relation.
- Demand as manifestation of passion.
- Phobia as localization of a more fundamental anxiety.
- Other's gaze.
- Symbolic castration as gap in knowledge.
- Hysteria's address to the Other and hystericization in treatment.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Klotz takes from Seminar XI the inseparability of transference, truth and deception, together with the relation of transference to knowledge. He supplements that framework with the three passions and with material from other periods of Lacan's teaching in order to show how affective intensity can be read structurally rather than treated as a psychological variable independent of language.

### Clinical example

The extended case of the hysterical woman with animal phobia is not presented as a completed treatment. Klotz explicitly states that he is reporting the first year of an analysis still in progress. Its function is therefore illustrative: to show how passion to know, phobic localization, anxiety, the gaze and the gap in knowledge can transform during transference.

### Interpretive status

The account of the clinical case and the linkage of passion to particular technical moments are Klotz's own analytic reconstruction. His use of later Lacanian claims concerning sexual nonrelation should not be retroactively confused with the exact conceptual vocabulary of Seminar XI itself.

### Sources used

- Jean-Pierre Klotz, 'The Passionate Dimension of Transference,' *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 101-107, printed pages 91-97.


## Marie-Hélène Brousse - The Drive (I)

**Author:** Marie-Hélène Brousse  
**Source location:** PDF pages 108-116; printed pages 99-107

### Governing question and thesis

Brousse begins with a question generated by Seminar XI's very architecture: **why is the drive one of Lacan's four fundamental concepts, while desire is not?** Her answer links doctrine, institutional history and analytic training. Seminar XI appears in 1964 after Lacan's exclusion from the International Psychoanalytical Association, at the same moment he is creating a new School. The return to Freud's four concepts therefore has a practical stake: what must be transmitted if psychoanalysis is to produce analysts rather than merely reproduce an institution?

Brousse treats the drive as a privileged point where Freud's discovery can be rearticulated through Lacan's theory of the signifier. Desire, especially the **analyst's desire**, is more specifically Lacan's invention. The drive supplies the Freudian term through which Lacan can reconstruct sexuality, transference and the unconscious while also transforming their relations.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 108 | PRINTED PAGE 99]

### 1964: excommunication, the School and the future of psychoanalysis

Brousse reads the opening chapter, 'Excommunication,' together with Lacan's 1964 **Founding Act**. Both ask what is fundamental to analytic practice and how the training of analysts should be organized after the institutional rupture with the International Psychoanalytical Association.

The distinction between an **institute** and a **School** is not terminological decoration. For Brousse, Lacan is attempting to invent a form of institution capable of transmitting psychoanalysis without reducing it to bureaucratic accreditation. The questions are practical: what counts as a training analysis, how can an analysis produce an analyst, and what relation should the analytic institution have to that production?

Lacan's solution is retroactive. An analysis cannot be certified as a training analysis solely because it was designated as such in advance. If it results in the production of an analyst, and that result can be interrogated through the School's forms of *controle* or supervision, then it will have functioned as a training analysis. The School therefore has an internal relation to the result but does not simply administer the analytic process from outside.

### Teaching as invention rather than repetition

Brousse gives equal weight to teaching. Psychoanalytic teaching cannot be identical with university teaching or the master's discourse. It must retain an inventive dimension. Freud invented psychoanalysis; Lacan did not regard his own task as simply repeating Freud; and the future of psychoanalysis requires further invention.

The **pass** belongs to this problem. Lacan proposes it as a procedure by which an analytic School might generate knowledge about what happens at the end of analysis and in the passage from analysand to analyst. Brousse therefore treats Seminar XI itself as a hinge: a way of anchoring a new analytic institution in Freud while reopening the question of what psychoanalysis is.

This institutional context explains the insistence on fundamentals. Lacan asks whether Freud's concepts are finished concepts, concepts still in formation, or concepts that require revision. The issue is not academic classification. It is what kind of conceptual trunk can moor a praxis and sustain the training of analysts.

### Freud's desire and the analyst's desire

Brousse highlights Lacan's question concerning **Freud's desire**: by what privilege was Freud's desire able to find the entrance into the field he called the unconscious? The question links discovery to the desire of the person who founds the field.

That immediately raises the corresponding question of Lacan's desire and, more generally, the desire of the analyst. Analytic training cannot be reduced to learning propositions because an analyst cannot be produced without a transformation or purification of desire.

This is also why Brousse thinks desire is absent from the official list of four fundamentals. Desire is not absent from Lacan's teaching; on the contrary, it is so specifically bound to Lacan's own invention, including the concept of the analyst's desire, that the Freudian drive becomes the better term through which to establish continuity and difference.

### Why the route to the drive passes through transference

Brousse turns to Chapter 12, 'Sexuality in the Defiles of the Signifier.' The table of contents itself is significant: the drive appears in a section called **'Transference and the Drive.'** The theoretical problem becomes how analysis moves from transference to drive.

Her first proposition is strong: there can be transference outside psychoanalysis, but there is no psychoanalytic unconscious without transference. Teaching, medicine and politics all mobilize transferential belief, but psychoanalysis uniquely makes transference the condition under which the unconscious is produced as analytic reality.

Freud did not invent transference in the way he invented the unconscious. He encountered transference as something that his method produced and with which it had to work.

### The two axes of transference: knowledge and love

Brousse distinguishes two axes that cannot be separated even though they pull in different directions.

The first is **knowledge**, linked to signifiers and repetition. A patient arrives with suffering. Choosing psychoanalysis and a particular analyst already involves transference. Under that supposition, suffering can be transformed into a symptom, that is, into something assumed to have meaning. The analyst is supposed to know what the symptom means. This is the facilitating side of transference.

The second axis is **love**, linked to being. Free association does not merely disclose information. It repeatedly undermines the speaker's ability to identify being with a stable signifier. A dream, slip or unexpected association shows that the meaning of one's own speech escapes. The unconscious therefore produces **subjective division** and *manque-a-etre*, lack of being or want-to-be.

Love emerges on the other side of that lack. Brousse formulates the relation sharply: **love gives being where analytic speech produces want-to-be**. Transference love is therefore not an arbitrary emotional disturbance added to analytic work. It is generated by the very operation that produces the unconscious.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 113 | PRINTED PAGE 104]

### 'The reality of the unconscious is sexual'

Brousse next reconstructs Lacan's declaration that the reality of the unconscious is sexual. She locates the Freudian stake in the break with Jung: Freud refused a desexualized libido. Lacan retains the sexual thesis but redefines what 'sexual' can mean once the human subject is constituted by the signifier.

She distinguishes two orders:

| Biological | Social / signifying |
|---|---|
| reproduction | alliance / affiliation |
| transmission of life | transmission of a name |
| need | drive |
| living being | subject |

The distinction draws on Levi-Strauss. Biological sexuality concerns reproduction and the transmission of life. Human social sexuality is also organized by kinship, alliance and the transmission of names, that is, by a combinatory of signifiers.

### Phallus: one signifier, not a male organ

The **phallus** is the privileged signifier in this organization, but Brousse insists that it is not identical with the male sexual organ. Biological reproduction gives two sexed poles, whereas Lacan's symbolic construction gives one privileged signifier. This is precisely why symbolic sexual difference cannot simply mirror anatomy.

Freud's Oedipal framework can permit an ambiguity between organ and signifier. Lacan's linguistic rereading separates them and treats the phallus as a signifier of difference and of a **loss or sacrifice of jouissance**. Speaking already entails that jouissance must be submitted to signification and cannot be wholly preserved.

In the period of Seminar XI this privileged metaphorization is organized by the **Name-of-the-Father**. Brousse adds a diachronic caution: late Lacan, especially after the work on Joyce, will relativize that privilege. The Name-of-the-Father remains the most common solution rather than the only possible one.

### Need, demand, drive and desire

Brousse then gives the core structural derivation. A biological need has an object. Hunger can be satisfied by milk. But the human infant receives milk from a speaking Other, through particular rhythms, prohibitions, timings and interpretations. Need is therefore taken into language and mediated by the **Other's demand**.

The signifier bars need. From the conjunction of need and the Other's demand comes the **drive**. Yet demand never coincides perfectly with need. Something escapes the correlation, and that remainder is **desire**.

The sequence can be summarized without treating it as a literal equation:

`need -> intervention of the Other's demand / signifier -> drive + remainder of desire`

The drive is thus neither instinct nor biological program. It is the effect of the signifier on need. Desire emerges from the loss produced in the same operation.

Brousse quotes Lacan's statement that the nodal point linking the pulsation of the unconscious to sexual reality is desire. Desire is therefore indispensable even though it is not named among the four fundamentals.

### Why every drive is partial

Once sexuality is organized through demand and the signifier, no drive can directly encode a natural male/female complementarity. The drive is **partial**. It is connected to local objects and to the Other's demand rather than to a complete instinctual program of genital relation.

This prepares Brousse's second lecture, where she will address Lacan's stronger proposition that every drive is virtually a death drive and will examine the object, the drive's circuit and the paradox of satisfaction.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Drive versus desire as candidates for a fundamental concept.
- Analytic training, School, *controle* and pass.
- Psychoanalytic teaching as invention.
- Freud's desire and analyst's desire.
- Transference as condition for production of the unconscious.
- Knowledge/repetition axis versus love/being axis of transference.
- Free association, subjective division and want-to-be.
- Biological sexuality versus social/signifying sexuality.
- Reproduction versus alliance/affiliation.
- Transmission of life versus transmission of a name.
- Need versus drive.
- Phallus as signifier rather than organ.
- Name-of-the-Father as privileged metaphorization in this period.
- Need, demand, drive and desire.
- Partial drive.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Brousse treats Seminar XI as simultaneously theoretical and institutional. Its four concepts are not an abstract canon but a way to re-ground analytic praxis after Lacan's exclusion. Her reading of Chapters 12-14 makes the transition from transference to drive depend on the production of unconscious knowledge, subjective division, transferential love and the signifier's transformation of biological need.

### Interpretive status

Brousse explicitly reads Seminar XI from later institutional and theoretical developments, including the pass, later Lacan on the Name-of-the-Father and later formulations of jouissance. Those retrospective comparisons are her interpretive framework and should not be treated as if every later distinction were already fully explicit in the 1964 seminar.

### Sources used

- Marie-Hélène Brousse, 'The Drive (I),' *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 108-116, printed pages 99-107.


## Marie-Hélène Brousse - The Drive (II)

**Author:** Marie-Hélène Brousse  
**Source location:** PDF pages 117-125; printed pages 109-117

### Governing question and thesis

Brousse's second lecture moves from the derivation of drive out of need and demand to the **object, satisfaction and circuit of the drive**. Her argument has three linked claims. First, neurotic fantasy initially confuses the cause of desire with what the subject imagines the Other demands. Second, the drive is a **montage**, not a biologically programmed instinct and not a representative of male/female complementarity. Third, analytic work moves from the object as demanded by the Other toward **object a as loss**, thereby exposing the subject's particular mode of jouissance.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 117 | PRINTED PAGE 109]

### The Other's demand and the constitution of the subject

Brousse begins by refining the previous lecture's formula. Need is barred through encounter with the Other's demand. The infant is constituted as a subject in a field already structured by signifiers. `S1-S2` can therefore be read as a representation of the signifying articulation of the Other's demand, while the barred subject is its effect.

Her clinical example is a woman unable to decide whether to have a child. The decisive remembered signifier of her mother's desire is the mother's furious cry to her children, **'I'm going to kill you.'** Brousse does not treat this as a transparent report of maternal intention. It is the signifier through which the patient has interpreted the Other's demand. The demand becomes, in the patient's structure, something like 'die.'

The patient's fantasy repeatedly stages her own disappearance. In love relationships she seeks the position of a discarded scrap or bad object, imagining herself lonely, abandoned and scorned. The example allows Brousse to show how the object in neurotic fantasy can become fused with the object the subject imagines the Other to be demanding.

### Drive formula and the neurotic fusion of demand with object a

The HTML-derived source damages the typography of Lacan's formulas, but Brousse explicitly invokes the **formula of the drive** and the **formula of fantasy**.

[FORMULA / MATHEME: Drive and fantasy]
Source location: PDF page 118, printed page 110.
Context: Brousse states that, in neurosis, the Other's lack is identified with the Other's demand. The object in fantasy therefore tends to be reduced to the object demanded by the Other.
Notation status: the source's custom mathematical glyphs are not reliably recoverable from the embedded text layer. Conventional Lacanian notation would distinguish the barred subject's relation to demand in the drive from `$ ◊ a` in fantasy, but this file preserves the conceptual relation rather than silently asserting damaged source glyphs.

The clinical consequence is important. In much object-relations literature, the object appears naturally as an object wanted by the mother or by the Other. Lacan's object a must instead be separated from this demanded object if desire is to be understood as caused by lack rather than simply by an interpersonal request.

### Separation from maternal demand

The Other's demand is sufficient to construct a drive, but not to produce the object that causes desire. For that, Brousse says, **separation** is required. If the child remains wholly the object of maternal demand, the child is devoted to what Lacan calls the mother's 'sexual service', meaning a libidinal function rather than genital sexuality.

Brousse gives the example of a psychotic girl and her mother. Their relation is experienced as a real bond with almost no space for separation. The mother continually touches the daughter and becomes intensely anxious whenever the girl achieves some independence. The daughter's physical inability to walk further reinforces the attachment.

The case is used structurally rather than moralistically. Brousse is showing what it means for the child to remain captured as object of the Other's satisfaction rather than to emerge through a separative operation as a subject related to a cause of desire.

She provocatively compares this structure with maternity and perversion, arguing that a perverse organization of relation to the object can find a socially sanctioned realization in maternity. This is Brousse's own interpretive extension and depends on distinctions she draws from later Lacan, including Seminar XX.

### The paradox of drive satisfaction

Brousse next takes up Lacan's four components of the drive: **source, pressure/impetus, object and aim**. Each demonstrates why drive is not instinct.

Pressure is constant rather than episodic. Consuming an object does not eliminate the drive's force in the manner hunger may be reduced by food. The object is not naturally matched to the drive. Milk corresponds biologically to hunger, but no naturally programmed object corresponds to the oral drive. The aim is not simply acquisition or consumption of a prey. Nor can the source be reduced to a biological trigger that determines the remaining components.

The consequence is the concept of **montage**. An instinct resembles a program coordinating organism and environment. A drive is assembled out of heterogeneous terms. It has no natural harmony that would guarantee a fit among pressure, source, object and aim.

### No genital drive and no natural sexual polarity

The drive is not organized by a male/female polarity. Nor can Freud's active/passive opposition simply replace male/female. If drive had a naturally genital organization, it could provide the unconscious with a complete program for complementary sexual relation. Lacan's insistence that the drives are partial denies such a program.

Biological sex remains real in the sense that an organism cannot simply disregard its material sexed characteristics. But this does not furnish an unconscious signifier that transparently declares someone male or female. Brousse uses transsexualism as an example of a confrontation among biological real, imaginary identification and symbolic conviction, while carefully distinguishing this from a psychoanalytic definition of sexuality.

The drive is therefore an apparatus that brings something of sexuality as real into symbolic and imaginary organization. Lacan says the drive in this sense **tricks the real**: by circling an object it captures a fragment within a signifying circuit.

### Partial objects and the hole

Brousse emphasizes that partial objects do not add up to a total object. The breast, feces, gaze, voice and related objects are not pieces from which complete genital sexuality could be assembled. Each is a local support for a circuit around lack.

Object a is therefore fundamentally linked to a **hole**. Images supplied by the subject's history veil the absence. Master signifiers and particular images can give the object a recognizable shape, but the structural object is not equivalent to those images.

This also links fantasy and object choice. What appears as the subject's 'favorite' object is a historically specific veil around an empty place.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 122 | PRINTED PAGE 114]

### Lamella, libido and death drive

Brousse turns to Lacan's myth of the **lamella**, the fantastical extra-flat, amoeba-like organ that survives division and cannot be destroyed in the way a sexed organism can. Lacan identifies this impossible organ with libido.

The myth separates libido from biological reproduction. Biological life begins and ends; libido figures an indestructible life detached from the reproductive cycle. But this indestructibility exists only as a representation produced through the symbolic order.

That is why Brousse connects libido to death. Representation presupposes the death or absence of the thing represented. The symbolic order is marked by this relation to death, so the drive constituted in the symbolic order is virtually a **death drive**. Brousse contrasts this with Freud's opposition between life drives and death drive: Lacan radicalizes the death-drive dimension by treating every drive as structurally implicated in it.

### From the Other's demand to object a and jouissance

Brousse marks an important chronological issue. In the formulation she is reconstructing, drive is initially written through the barred subject and demand, both on the symbolic side. Later Lacanian developments give the real and **jouissance** a more explicit place through object a.

Analytic work can be described as a movement from the imagined object of the Other's demand toward the bare object as loss. The analysand initially hears almost anything the analyst says or does as a demand. Even silence can be heard as an order to speak or to stop speaking. Brousse's humorous example is a patient whose vacation is spoiled because her simple wish that he 'have a good vacation' is interpreted as mockery and as a demand that he not go.

Work on fantasy gradually disconnects the object from this constructed demand. At the limit, the Other is revealed not to have been demanding the absolute object the subject organized a life around. The object appears as an emptiness or loss rather than a positive command. **Anxiety** indicates proximity to this object because the familiar veil is weakening.

### `Se faire`: beyond active and passive

Lacan's French reflexive expression **`se faire`**, roughly 'to get oneself [done/seen/eaten/heard...]', allows Brousse to show why drive cannot be organized by the simple active/passive opposition. To 'make oneself understood' requires both an active maneuver and dependence on another who completes the action.

The same grammar appears in colloquial sexual expressions. Drive satisfaction uses the Other's demand as the circuit through which satisfaction can be obtained. `Se faire` is therefore a linguistic emblem of the drive's montage: the subject introduces satisfaction into the field of the Other while simultaneously occupying an object-position within that circuit.

### Kris's plagiarism case: interpretation must reach the drive

The final clinical argument comes from Ernst Kris's famous case. A patient complains that his ideas are plagiarized. Kris checks the patient's writing and reassures him that the ideas are original, interpreting the plagiarism fear as a defense against recognizing his own creativity. After the session, however, the patient reports an urge to go to a restaurant and eat **fresh brains**.

Lacan treats this as acting out and as a critique of Kris's interpretation. Kris has interpreted an ego defense instead of the drive. The fresh-brains scene returns what the interpretation missed.

Brousse links the case to **mental anorexia**. The relevant object is not simply 'ideas' but *nothing* as object: having no ideas, eating nothing, producing nothing. As in anorexia, the subject may defend not by refusing an object but by making **nothing itself** the object of a satisfaction.

Interpretation must therefore reach the subject's mode of jouissance and the object structure of fantasy, not only decode metaphorical signifiers or strengthen the ego. If analysis were merely symptom plus interpretation, Brousse says, it could resemble a hard science of meanings. The drive interrupts that model by introducing the heterogeneous object and satisfaction.

### Fundamental fantasy and change in jouissance

Brousse ends by restating the trajectory of analysis: from object as **Other's demand** to object as **loss**, object a. Once the subject's relation to object a becomes isolable, the drive cannot be separated from the fundamental fantasy. Work on fantasy may then permit a change in the subject's position of jouissance.

This is the deepest reason the drive is fundamental. It marks the point at which signifying interpretation alone is insufficient and analytic practice has to address satisfaction, loss and the object.

### Major concepts and distinctions

- Drive as effect of the Other's demand on need.
- Subject constituted by signifiers of the Other's demand.
- Neurotic fusion of object a with the demanded object.
- Separation from maternal demand.
- Drive versus instinct.
- Source, pressure, object and aim.
- Montage versus biological program.
- Partial drive and absence of genital drive.
- Drive as apparatus that 'tricks the real'.
- Partial object versus total object.
- Hole and object a.
- Lamella and libido.
- Every drive as virtually a death drive.
- Object as demand versus object as loss.
- Anxiety as proximity to object a.
- `Se faire` beyond active/passive polarity.
- Acting out and Kris's fresh-brains case.
- Nothing as object in mental anorexia.
- Drive, fantasy and jouissance.

### Relation to Seminar XI

Brousse closely follows Chapters 13 and 14, 'The Deconstruction of the Drive' and 'The Partial Drive and its Circuit.' Her distinctive contribution is to connect those chapters to separation, clinical examples and the later Lacanian vocabulary of object a and jouissance. She emphasizes that Seminar XI's drive theory prevents psychoanalysis from becoming a hermeneutics of signifiers alone.

### Interpretive status

Several of Brousse's formulations explicitly use later Lacan to read Seminar XI, including the stronger emphasis on jouissance, the relation to Seminar XX and later teaching on the Name-of-the-Father. These diachronic comparisons are analytically useful but should not be collapsed into the vocabulary of the 1964 seminar itself.

### Sources used

- Marie-Hélène Brousse, 'The Drive (II),' *Reading Seminar XI*, PDF pages 117-125, printed pages 109-117.


## Maire Jaanus - The Démontage of the Drive

**Author:** Maire Jaanus  
**Source location:** PDF pages 126-143; printed pages 119-136

### Governing question and thesis

Jaanus offers one of the volume's most expansive readings of the drive. Taking Lacan's French title *Démontage de la pulsion* literally as a **dismantling or disassembly** of the drive, she argues that Seminar XI cuts the body into two heterogeneous corporeal logics: a **body of instinct/need** and a **body of drive/want**. The drive is not a refined instinct. It is a montage produced where bodily real, erogenous loss, language and relation to the Other intersect.

Her essay then pushes Lacan's account in a distinctive philosophical direction. Object a is tied to real bodily losses, the drive's reflexive circuit becomes a primitive mode of subjectification, and the lamella is read as the myth of an **immortal libido** whose loss makes sexual mortality possible. The resulting account ranges well beyond an exposition of Seminar XI and should be read as Jaanus's theoretical extension of it.

[SOURCE PDF PAGE 126 | PRINTED PAGE 119]

### Two bodies beneath the mirror image

Jaanus begins from the history of Lacan's body theory. In the mirror-stage period, the decisive opposition was between the unified image and the fragmented body. Seminar XI, she argues, makes another cut. Beneath the specular body appear a **body of instincts** and a **body of drives**.

She compares the two levels to a palimpsest or pentimento. One bodily organization is drawn over another without entirely erasing it. Instinct, drive and desire can therefore coexist as layers whose different logics sometimes show through one another.

The body of instinct is organized by **need** in the strong sense of necessity for self-preservation. Its privileged sources are the inner organs: stomach, intestines, bladder and other systems whose pressures periodically demand discharge or replenishment. The body of drive is organized around **want, lack and erogenous requirement**, especially the rims and openings where inside and outside meet.

Jaanus relates this distinction to Merleau-Ponty's 'flesh' but refuses to make language and libido two reversible sides of one substance. Lacan's bodily real and the order of words remain heterogeneous even when they cross.

### Homeostatic pleasure versus erotic forcing

Both instinct and drive involve pleasure, but not the same economy. Need can be satisfied homeostatically. Hunger rises and falls; a full bladder is emptied; the organism returns toward equilibrium. Jaanus calls this a kind of **shock-pleasure**, the relief of a periodic pressure.

Drive operates differently. Following Lacan's insistence that drive is not reducible to *Drang* as a momentary thrust, she emphasizes Freud's characterization of drive as **constant force**. It has no day or night, no seasonal rhythm and no point at which satisfaction simply switches it off.
