# 13. Common Markets and Segregation

Author: Marie-Helene Brousse

Source span:
- Printed pp. 254-262
- PDF pp. 263-271

## 1. Orientation and central thesis

Brousse begins from Lacan's injunction that the analyst must be able to encounter the subjectivity of his or her time. Psychoanalysis has a distinctive clinical setting, but the analysand's discourse brings into treatment the imaginary, symbolic, and real coordinates of an era. For Brousse, the early twenty-first century is marked by technological, economic, political, and scientific changes that have altered the real to which clinical practice responds.

Her central thesis is that the contemporary master's discourse is no longer best modeled by a paternal, hierarchical authority. The new master is universalizing and horizontal. Its commanding signifier is the market, more precisely the common or global market, while its corresponding knowledge consists of procedures, protocols, evaluations, and standardized management. This reorganization does not eliminate segregation. On the contrary, Brousse follows Lacan in arguing that universalization produces a harsher, ramified segregation as its underside.

The clinical consequence is equally important. If an epoch's clinic corresponds to the master's discourse of that epoch, then the movement from Name-of-the-Father, prohibition, and classification toward market universality, protocols, and evaluation changes symptoms, transference, and the subject's modes of satisfaction. Brousse proposes a contemporary application of the master's discourse in which the global market functions as S1, procedures and protocols as S2, the connected subject as the barred subject, and segregation as the mode of surplus jouissance represented by objet a.

[Source: printed pp. 254-255 / PDF pp. 263-264]

## 2. Argument structure

### 2.1 The analyst and the subjectivity of the epoch

Brousse's point of departure is Lacan's 1953 claim that the analyst must know the symbolic movement of the era in which subjects live. This is not a call for sociological commentary to replace clinical work. It is a condition for understanding the coordinates that an analysand brings into speech.

She argues that earlier conceptual frameworks no longer organize contemporary social reality as effectively as they once did. The postwar transformation of politics, the collapse of state Marxist utopias, the rise of religious fundamentalism and terrorism, technological acceleration, and the increasing social authority of science all contribute to what she calls a modified real.

The common tendency of these transformations is universalization. Capitalism aims toward a single market; technology aims toward universal diffusion; science addresses itself to universally valid knowledge. The world increasingly presents itself as if the same truth, procedures, products, and criteria should apply everywhere.

[Source: printed pp. 254-255 / PDF pp. 263-264]

### 2.2 A modified real after war, science, and globalization

Brousse reads Lacan's 1947 text on British psychiatry and the war as an early diagnosis of the new period. Lacan had already warned that the major dangers to humanity would not simply come from unruly individuals but from the conjunction of superegoic powers, mass submission, manipulated images, passions, and the abandonment of conscience.

Brousse brings this warning into the present. Fanatical sacrifice and the capacity to manipulate populations show that conformity can be more dangerous than individual unruliness. Scientific and technical means of acting on the psyche make the manipulation of judgment and passion a central political problem.

She also cautions against assuming that ethics committees and legal procedures solve the problem created by scientific universalization. Psychoanalysis occupies a singular ethical position because it does not direct the subject's life according to social or moral norms. The analyst directs the treatment, not the analysand's choices. A symptom is constructed through the subject's speech, and a solution is analytic only if the subject invents it.

[Source: printed pp. 255-256 / PDF pp. 264-265]

### 2.3 Psychoanalysis at the excluded edge of scientific universality

Brousse emphasizes the paradoxical relation between psychoanalysis and science. Psychoanalysis became possible through scientific medicine, yet it emerged precisely where medicine excluded phenomena it could not incorporate. Hysterical symptoms, treated as simulation or fakery when they failed to match biological knowledge, became the site of Freud's discovery of unconscious phenomena.

Psychoanalysis therefore remains linked to scientific modernity while treating what the universalizing operation of science leaves out. Its method is rational, but its ethical wager is on the singular subject excluded by universal knowledge. For Brousse, this position gives psychoanalysis a distinctive task in relation to the contemporary master's discourse.

[Source: printed p. 256 / PDF p. 265]

### 2.4 The therapeutic as contemporary universal

Brousse identifies the therapeutic as one of the major contemporary universals. Experiences once managed by moral, religious, familial, or ordinary social frameworks are increasingly redescribed as objects of therapeutic care. Trauma is an obvious example, but the same tendency extends to everyday problems of work, love, and family life.

She connects this with Freud's observation that ethics can function as a therapeutic attempt by means of the superego. In contemporary Western societies, the therapeutic has increasingly displaced traditional moral and religious management of suffering. This destabilizes the boundary of mental illness. If every disturbance in desire or satisfaction calls for therapy, the category of illness becomes difficult to delimit.

Brousse makes a two-sided argument. The success of scientific medicine encourages belief that suffering can be cured by the correct molecule, operation, or procedure. Yet scientific medicine also narrows its legitimate field by requiring specific biological or empirical criteria. The resulting gap allows the therapeutic to detach from medicine and become a general social regulatory function. Psychotherapy can then serve the contemporary master as a cushion of compassion, managing the suffering produced by social arrangements without necessarily questioning those arrangements.

[Source: printed pp. 256-257 / PDF pp. 265-266]

### 2.5 The four discourses as a formal tool for social change

Brousse turns explicitly to the matheme of the four discourses. From 1968 onward, Lacan formalizes social bonds through four positions and four terms. The master's discourse is characterized by a commanding signifier in the agent position.

The classical examples of S1 are imperatives. Brousse mentions commands such as "Get rich!" and "Move on!" to show that the master signifier changes with social organization. Her hypothesis is that under the contemporary hegemony of capitalism, the dominant S1 is the market, more specifically the common market.

She connects this directly to Lacan's 1967 proposition that the future would be one of common markets. By the early 2000s, Brousse argues, this future has become a global political and economic reality. Globalization presents itself as an empire that is unique without thereby becoming genuinely common. Products and profits are expected to circulate without limit.

[Source: printed p. 258 / PDF p. 267]

### 2.6 Procedures and protocols as S2

If the market is the contemporary master signifier, Brousse asks what knowledge corresponds to it. Her answer is procedures and protocols. Modern corporations and institutions extract practical know-how from agents, formalize it, computerize it, and reinject it as standardized procedures for the execution of tasks.

Her examples range from retail chains to cancer treatment, aviation, policing, and administrative practice. Taylorism is the ancestor of this development, but contemporary procedures are far more precise and extensive. Research gathers data about behavior and performance, turns those data into formal knowledge, and then returns that knowledge to the field as a universal protocol.

This S2 serves the management of the market. Human activity is increasingly calibrated according to maximum output or profit and minimum cost. The relation between S1 and S2 therefore defines a modern master that is less visibly hierarchical than the old paternal master but no less effective.

[Source: printed pp. 258-259 / PDF pp. 267-268]

### 2.7 From authoritarian master to liberal master

Drawing on Jacques-Alain Miller's distinction between authoritarian and liberal masters, Brousse contrasts two structures of power. The authoritarian master is modeled on the father or chief and operates vertically through command and sanction. The liberal master emerges from the horizontal universality of markets and procedures.

This changes surveillance and punishment. Instead of a superior authority inspecting subordinates, evaluation becomes generalized and can ideally be carried out by peers or even by machines. Diagnostic classification offers an analogous model: if the correct manual exists, the subject can theoretically be sorted without a privileged interpreter.

Brousse sees this as a major clinical shift. Classical Lacanian practice had the Name-of-the-Father as its pivot and classified subjects according to their relation to it. The contemporary master's discourse does not disappear when paternal authority weakens; it relocates regulation into procedures, evaluation, circulation, and market norms.

[Source: printed pp. 259-260 / PDF pp. 268-269]

### 2.8 The clinic changes with the master's discourse

Brousse explicitly states that the clinic of an epoch corresponds to the master's discourse of that epoch. If the master's discourse changes, symptoms and transferential modalities also change. The passage from the Name-of-the-Father toward the market means that regulation of jouissance is less visibly organized through prohibition and classification and more through evaluation and procedure.

The contemporary subject is accordingly modeled as a subject in a system. The subject receives a place through flows of information, products, and profits and can connect with others with few limits beyond technical access. Brousse calls this an autarchic subject plugged into universally accessible chatter and knowledge. The subject is less obviously located by fixed symbolic positions in kinship and less transparently organized by classical Oedipal coordinates.

[Source: printed p. 260 / PDF p. 269]

### 2.9 Universalization produces segregation

The weakening or evaporation of the paternal function does not yield simple homogenization. Brousse relies on Lacan's 1968 remark that the scar left by the evaporation of the father can be grouped under the heading of segregation. Universal communication and universalism appear to dissolve barriers, yet they produce more numerous and ramified segregations.

For Brousse, this segregation is a regime of satisfaction. On one side is the connected subject who can circulate through universal systems. On the other is the speaking being reduced to a product and attached to localized modes of jouissance. Universal market equivalence and particular communities of enjoyment therefore grow together rather than cancelling each other.

She recalls Lacan's 1967 warning that the reorganization of social groups by science and common markets would find its equilibrium in a harsher extension of segregation. Her example from James Ellroy describes parallel worlds organized by different signifiers and surplus jouissances, worlds that meet only in disruptive acts. Where a single prohibition or paternal limit once seemed to organize a field, multiple limits and communities now proliferate.

[Source: printed pp. 260-261 / PDF pp. 269-270]

### 2.10 Brousse's proposed matheme of the postmodern master

Brousse ends by mapping her hypothesis directly onto the master's discourse.

The general places of discourse are:

```text
agent -> work
truth    production
```

The master's discourse is:

```text
S1 -> S2
$     a
```

Her proposed contemporary application is:

```text
global market -> procedures and protocols
     (S1)               (S2)

subject in a system     segregation
       ($)                  (a)
```

Above the bar are the universalizing elements generated through the reorganization of human phenomena by science: the global market and procedural knowledge. Below the bar are the divided subject and the segregated modes of jouissance that universalization produces as its underside.

Brousse describes the contemporary subject as both connected and isolated. The subject can enter universal networks of communication while belonging to increasingly differentiated communities organized around identity, objects, and modes of satisfaction. She lists communities such as gay, lesbian, Black, Latino, WASP, Alcoholics Anonymous, and Narcotics Anonymous to illustrate the multiplication of groups, each with its own objects and signifiers.

Her conclusion is concise: these are the structural coordinates of modern clinical practice.

[Source: printed pp. 261-262 / PDF pp. 270-271]

## 3. Key Lacanian concepts

### Subjectivity of the epoch

The analyst must be able to read the symbolic and real coordinates that organize contemporary subjects. This does not replace singular analysis with sociology; it is a condition for understanding the social signifiers and modes of jouissance that appear in treatment.

### Master signifier, S1

For Brousse, S1 is historically variable. The contemporary candidate is the global or common market, whose imperative organizes circulation and evaluation across domains.

### Knowledge, S2

Procedures, protocols, codes, statistical knowledge, and standardized forms of evaluation constitute the knowledge corresponding to the market master signifier. They are extracted from practice and returned as universal rules.

### Name-of-the-Father

The Name-of-the-Father is the pivot of the classical clinic Brousse contrasts with the present. Its reduced organizing power does not abolish mastery. It changes how jouissance is regulated and how clinical phenomena present themselves.

### Segregation and objet a

Segregation is the underside of universalization. Brousse places it in the product position associated with objet a and surplus jouissance. Universal markets and scientific procedures therefore coexist with increasingly particularized communities of enjoyment.

### Evaluation

Evaluation is a central mechanism of the liberal master. Unlike traditional vertical inspection, it can be distributed horizontally among peers or automated. Its apparent neutrality conceals its role in regulating subjects according to market and procedural norms.

## 4. Relation to Seminar XVII

Brousse uses the four-discourse formalization as a tool for diagnosing a change in mastery. Seminar XVII supplies the structural matrix: S1, S2, divided subject, objet a, agent, work, truth, and production. Her distinctive move is to insert contemporary terms into this matrix rather than merely restate Lacan's examples.

The proposed mapping of global market to S1 and procedures/protocols to S2 is Brousse's hypothesis. Likewise, the pairing of subject-in-a-system with the divided subject and segregation with objet a is her contemporary application of the master's discourse.

Her broader claim that the clinic changes with the master's discourse connects Seminar XVII to later discussions of the decline or evaporation of paternal authority. She does not say that social change erases structure. She argues that the same formal positions can be occupied by different historical operators and therefore generate different clinical presentations.

## 5. Examples, interlocutors and external references

Brousse's primary references are Lacan, Freud, Jacques-Alain Miller, and Eric Laurent. Lacan's postwar writings on British psychiatry, the 1967 Proposition, the 1968 note on the father and universalism, and Seminar XVII provide the main Lacanian base. Freud's *Civilization and Its Discontents* supports the relation between ethics, the superego, and the therapeutic.

Jean-Claude Maleval appears in relation to the proliferation of diagnostic categories. Miller supplies the distinction between authoritarian and liberal masters and the claim that classical Lacanian diagnosis was organized around the Name-of-the-Father. Brousse also refers to Taylorism, Charles Chaplin's *Modern Times*, corporate procedure, standardized medicine, and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual as examples of procedural S2.

Her political and economic references include globalization, the common market, terrorism, scientific universalization, and the use of evaluation across institutions. James Ellroy provides a literary example for the coexistence of separate worlds of jouissance.

## 6. Mathemes, formulas, figures and diagrams

The essay explicitly reproduces the general discourse positions:

```text
agent -> work
truth    production
```

It then gives the master's discourse:

```text
S1 -> S2
$     a
```

Finally, Brousse proposes a contemporary application:

```text
global market -> procedures and protocols
     S1                  S2

subject in a system     segregation
       $                    a
```

This last arrangement is an interpretive application by Brousse, not a formula presented by Lacan in Seminar XVII under those labels.

[Source: printed pp. 258-261 / PDF pp. 267-270]

## 7. Interpretive contribution and limits

Brousse's most distinctive claim is that the global market can be treated as the contemporary master signifier and procedural knowledge as its S2. This enables her to explain how mastery can become more universal, horizontal, and apparently impersonal without disappearing.

A second contribution is the identification of evaluation as a contemporary technology of power. It replaces or supplements the paternal inspection and prohibition characteristic of the authoritarian master. Its horizontal and automated form can make mastery appear neutral even while it standardizes subjects.

A third contribution is the link between universalization and segregation. Brousse does not treat identity-based or enjoyment-based communities as simply remnants of a pre-global world. She presents them as products of the universalizing process itself. The more the market and science impose common procedures, the more particular modes of jouissance can crystallize into segregated groups.

Her clinical conclusion follows from this social hypothesis. The classical Name-of-the-Father-centered clinic cannot simply be applied unchanged if the forms of mastery regulating contemporary subjects have shifted. This is an interpretive program for contemporary Lacanian practice, not a direct empirical conclusion established by Seminar XVII alone.

# 14. The Intimate, the Extimate, and Psychoanalytic Discourse

Author: Pierre-Gilles Gueguen

Source span:
- Printed pp. 263-273
- PDF pp. 272-282

## 1. Orientation and central thesis

Gueguen distinguishes several uses of intimacy and truth in literature and psychoanalysis in order to clarify Lacan's neologism "extimacy." Autobiographical writing has made the public exposure of private life an aesthetic and cultural value, and psychoanalysis also summons intimate material. Yet analytic intimacy is not equivalent to confession, self-revelation, or the literary display of what convention hides. Nor is extimacy simply a more profound intimacy.

His central thesis is that psychoanalysis changes the status of truth. The analysand begins with a search for truth, but analytic experience shows that truth cannot be possessed or fully stated. In later Lacan, truth can only be half-said and is bound to jouissance. The intimate material of an analysis is therefore valuable not because it is secret or scandalous, but because it can reveal the subject's singular signifying constellation and relation to the Other.

Extimacy goes further. It concerns what is most intimate yet structurally exterior to the subject's self-representation: the cause of desire, the drive, jouissance, and objet a. Gueguen connects extimacy with the end of analysis, the pass, the analyst's desire, and the analyst's discourse. The endpoint is not expert knowledge or autobiographical transparency. It is an analytic solitude in which the subject encounters a noncollectivizable relation to the cause of jouissance and can take up the position of analyst without pretending to master psychoanalytic truth.

[Source: printed pp. 263-264 / PDF pp. 272-273]

## 2. Argument structure

### 2.1 Literary intimacy and the public use of private truth

Gueguen begins with Rousseau, especially *Confessions* and *Reveries of a Solitary Walker*. These works bring intimacy into literature but do so in different ways. In *Confessions*, the project is to say everything and use truth as a weapon against judgment and persecution. The exposure of what decorum and shame normally hide becomes a way of placing the self beyond the Other's verdict.

In *Reveries*, the relation changes. Rousseau retreats from social judgment and constructs an internal solitude in which he can enjoy himself despite others. Gueguen notes the clinical precision of this formulation because the new intimacy is tied to a specific arrangement of jouissance rather than simply to disclosure.

The nineteenth-century journal intime and later autobiographical literature continue the traffic in truth. Amiel, Gide, romantic and modern writers, and the literature of confession all address a reader, even when they celebrate solitude. Truth is transmitted under the gaze of an Other, whether posterity, the bourgeois public, or an imagined sympathetic reader.

This means literary intimacy always involves an economy of address. It can challenge shame, cultivate transgression, authenticate a singular self, or arrange a new relation between the writer and society. Even artistic solitude remains supported by the consistency of an other who reads.

[Source: printed pp. 263-265 / PDF pp. 272-274]

### 2.2 The fascination with hidden truth

Gueguen warns against assuming that whatever is hidden is therefore more true. Literary intimacy often relies on the idea that what convention conceals must contain the key to the subject. This encourages a will to say everything, especially what shame and semblants require to remain veiled.

For psychoanalysis this can be misleading. Jouissance is certainly at stake in what subjects hide, but analysis is not a hunt for a secret kernel waiting to be exposed. The analytic relation to truth cannot be reduced to stripping away appearances until a final hidden content is uncovered.

[Source: printed p. 265 / PDF p. 274]

### 2.3 Analytic uses of the intimate: truth as surprise and half-saying

Analysis begins, at least phenomenologically, as a search for truth. Yet truth emerges unpredictably. It surprises, produces effects, and cannot be handled like a stable object. Gueguen invokes the Heideggerian distinction between truth as adequation and truth as unveiling to clarify Lacan's trajectory.

Later Lacan goes beyond a simple ideal of unveiling. Truth can only be half-said and is the sister of jouissance. This limit belongs to the logic of psychoanalysis itself: a consistent system marks its own incompleteness. Truth therefore cannot provide a complete metalanguage in which the subject's life is finally rendered transparent.

Freud's rule of analytic frankness might appear to demand complete confession. The analysand is asked not to censor indecent or apparently irrelevant thoughts. But Gueguen insists that analytic speech is not Rousseau's combative claim to possess the truth. The analysand abandons himself to the Other that speaks through him. Fiction itself matters because unconscious constructions rationalize the sexual impasse and the impossible around which the subject's history is organized.

The analyst accordingly rejects direction of conscience. The treatment remains oriented toward truth, but not toward moral avowal or confession. The point is to let the subject encounter the effects of unconscious knowledge and the sexual impasse that those effects articulate.

[Source: printed pp. 266-267 / PDF pp. 275-276]

### 2.4 The analyzing use of truth and the pass

Gueguen then distinguishes different facets of analytic truth. The first is the analyzing use: within treatment, the subject encounters truth effects that diverge from conscious prejudices and reveal what the subject has been for the Other.

The pass adds another operation. In the pass, the analysand presents a case to passers. The resulting intimacy is not the intimacy of confession or the recovery of a primitive hidden fact. It is the presentation of a singular signifying constellation that has become legible through analysis.

The passand must show how discontinuous signifying elements form a coherent structure of unconscious knowledge. This does not require saying everything. Gueguen stresses reduction rather than exhaustive disclosure: everything necessary must be said, not every biographical detail.

The institutional procedure therefore transforms intimacy into transmissible analytic knowledge. A particular case contributes a new version of the relation between a subject and semblants. The analyst functions as guarantor of the barred Other and as the element that anchors meaning precisely because the Other is incomplete.

[Source: printed pp. 267-268 / PDF pp. 276-277]

### 2.5 Testimony and the Analyst of the School

Gueguen distinguishes a third use of truth: the public testimonial of an appointed Analyst of the School. Here the singular case is not merely recounted. It is worked so that its construction can contribute to psychoanalytic knowledge more generally.

The task is to move from the singular toward a paradigm without dissolving singularity into a universal law. The case can illuminate clinical problems and produce lessons for psychoanalysis while remaining rooted in a particular analytic trajectory.

This stage may yield what Gueguen calls, following Lacan, a new signifier. The truth of the intimate experience becomes a discreet but indispensable fulcrum for explaining what an analysis does and what problems analytic practice raises.

[Source: printed p. 269 / PDF p. 278]

### 2.6 Extimacy is not intensified intimacy

The term extimacy is a Lacanian neologism later developed by Jacques-Alain Miller. Gueguen insists that it was not coined as a symmetrical opposite of intimacy, nor does it mean the deepest hidden interior.

Intimate and extimate can both designate what is closest and most hidden, but they differ structurally. The intimate often concerns something the subject withholds, shelters, or exposes selectively in order to preserve semblants and modesty. The extimate concerns what is not simply concealed but difficult or impossible for the subject to articulate because it lies beyond the plane of identifications and familiar self-representation.

To approach extimacy is therefore to approach the cause of desire and the drive. This makes objet a a privileged term, though Gueguen repeats Miller's warning that objet a itself is also a semblant. Extimacy concerns less the Other's desire than the Other's jouissance, especially where the Other does not exist as a complete guarantor.

[Source: printed pp. 269-270 / PDF pp. 278-279]

### 2.7 Extimacy, the analyst, and the remainder of analysis

From the perspective of the end of analysis, Gueguen links extimacy to the analyst not as placeholder for a lacking Other but as positive remainder of the analytic operation. The analyst has functioned as partner of the drive.

This is a decisive shift. The extimate is not a final hidden meaning decoded by interpretation. It concerns the cause of jouissance. Gueguen leaves open whether it can be fully said at all. Like truth, it is transmitted through half-saying and may appear as paradox, contradiction, joke, or a formulation of an impossible specific to the case.

The treatment isolates the substances and signifying supports through which the drive has operated, but those supports are not the ultimate aim. Lacan's term objet a names the cause that cannot be reduced to any one empirical object.

The intimate testimony of analysis can be multiple and narrative. Extimacy allows access to a One that is singular and cannot be collectivized. This One does not ground a new universal identity. It marks the subject's nonexchangeable relation to jouissance.

[Source: printed pp. 270-271 / PDF pp. 279-280]

### 2.8 Analytic solitude and the analyst's discourse

Gueguen links extimacy to the analysand's approach to being and to the question of becoming an analyst. At the end of the analytic trajectory, the subject encounters the analyst's desire and enters what he calls analytic solitude.

This solitude is not Rousseauian withdrawal from society. It is the position required by the analyst's discourse, which Lacan distinguishes from the discourse of someone who is merely analyzing. The analyst cannot rely on the social guarantees of expertise, accumulated knowledge, or professional effectiveness.

The analyst's discourse is therefore not the discourse of a specialist who has an authoritative opinion on every matter, nor the self-certification of a practitioner who justifies an act by saying it works. It requires a capacity to distinguish, case by case, what belongs to analytic discourse and what belongs to the social field. That judgment cannot be generated by a universal protocol because it depends on the singular pathways of a properly conducted analysis.

The Analyst of the School thus occupies an unstable position. Appointment opens a possibility rather than guaranteeing success. Training and completed analysis are necessary, but no accumulated experience removes the risk of a false step.

[Source: printed pp. 271-272 / PDF pp. 280-281]

## 3. Key Lacanian concepts

### Truth

Gueguen follows Lacan from truth as unveiling toward truth as half-saying. Truth is indispensable to analysis but cannot become complete knowledge. Its limit is bound to jouissance and to the incompleteness of the symbolic.

### Intimacy

Analytic intimacy is not simply private content. It concerns the singular constellation of signifiers through which the subject's unconscious knowledge is organized. The analytic use of intimacy is oriented toward structure and transmission rather than confession.

### Extimacy

Extimacy names what is most intimate while also being structurally exterior to the ego's self-recognition. It concerns the cause of desire, the drive, and jouissance beyond the subject's ordinary identifications.

### Objet a

Objet a is central to Gueguen's account because it names the cause of desire and the remainder around which extimacy is organized. He also preserves Miller's caution that objet a is itself a semblant rather than an unmediated substance.

### Barred Other

The analytic relation is supported by the fact that the Other is incomplete. The analyst does not restore a complete Other but can function in a way that makes its lack operative.

### Pass and testimony

The pass transforms the intimate material of analysis into a transmissible construction. Testimony does not require exhaustive confession. It reduces the case to the signifying and logical elements necessary to show how the subject's position was organized and altered.

### Analyst's discourse

The analyst's discourse is not expert discourse. It is a position that depends on the analyst's relation to the remainder of analysis, the analyst's desire, and the singularity of each case.

## 4. Relation to Seminar XVII

Gueguen's direct connection to Seminar XVII centers on truth, jouissance, the analyst's discourse, and Lacan's distinction between analytic and analyzing discourse. Seminar XVII provides the background for treating truth as limited, for locating the analyst outside ordinary mastery, and for linking the analyst's position to a structural remainder rather than to complete knowledge.

The essay also draws on later and earlier Lacanian materials, especially *Encore*, *Television*, "Direction of the Treatment," and the 1967 Proposition. Its account of extimacy is explicitly mediated by Jacques-Alain Miller's development of the term. The resulting argument is therefore not a chapter-by-chapter exposition of Seminar XVII but a focused elaboration of issues that the seminar makes central to analytic discourse.

## 5. Examples, interlocutors and external references

Rousseau is the principal literary example. *Confessions* represents a truth addressed to and weaponized against the Other; *Reveries* represents a more solitary arrangement of enjoyment. Gueguen also cites Amiel, Gide, Baudelaire, Rimbaud, Conrad, Cendrars, and Celine to map literary modes of intimacy.

He uses Jean Starobinski on Rousseau, Heidegger and Jean Beaufret on truth as unveiling, Freud on analytic frankness, and Jacques-Alain Miller on extimacy, the barred Other, desire, and jouissance. The institutional practices of the pass and the Analyst of the School provide the specifically psychoanalytic examples.

## 6. Mathemes, formulas, figures and diagrams

The essay does not introduce a new diagram. Its key formal references are conceptual relations among the barred Other, objet a, desire, jouissance, and the analyst's discourse.

Gueguen distinguishes two interpretations of the barred Other, following Miller: one through the Other's desire and another through the Other's jouissance. Extimacy concerns the latter. This distinction should be preserved as an interpretive axis rather than converted into a new formula not supplied by the essay.

## 7. Interpretive contribution and limits

Gueguen's first distinctive contribution is to separate psychoanalytic intimacy from literary confession. The analytic value of intimate material does not come from scandal, depth, or exhaustive disclosure. It comes from how singular signifiers and unconscious knowledge can be reduced, articulated, and transmitted.

His second contribution is the clarification of extimacy. Extimacy is not a superlative intimacy. It names the subject's relation to a cause of desire and jouissance that is both closest and structurally outside egoic self-possession.

A third contribution is the connection between extimacy and analytic formation. The end of analysis, the pass, public testimony, the analyst's desire, and the analyst's discourse form a sequence in which singularity becomes transmissible without becoming a universal expertise.

The essay's institutional claims belong to Gueguen's Lacanian orientation and to Miller's elaboration of the pass and extimacy. They should not be presented as unmediated statements from Seminar XVII alone.

## 8. Retrieval anchors

Retrieval anchors: Pierre-Gilles Gueguen; intimate; extimate; extimacy; truth; half-saying; jouissance; objet a; cause of desire; drive; barred Other; Other's desire; Other's jouissance; Rousseau; Confessions; Reveries; autobiography; analytic frankness; pass; passand; passers; Analyst of the School; testimony; analyst's desire; analytic solitude; analyst's discourse; semblant.

# 15. Bureaucratic Speech Acts and the University Discourse: Lacan's Theory of Modernity

Author: Geoff Boucher

Source span:
- Printed pp. 274-291
- PDF pp. 283-300

## 1. Orientation and central thesis

Boucher reconstructs Seminar XVII as a theory of modernity in which the traditional master is progressively displaced by bureaucracy and the growing authority of systematic knowledge. His central problem is bureaucratic rationalization: how can power become less visibly personal and political while becoming more pervasive through expert knowledge, institutional procedure, evaluation, and apparently neutral description?

He argues that Lacan's four discourses provide a structural matrix for answering this question. The university discourse does not simply replace the master's discourse in a linear philosophy of history. The four discourses can rotate contingently, and their relations form hegemonic articulations rather than a teleology. Still, modernity gives increasing weight to the university discourse, especially to science, technology, bureaucracy, and expert administration. The ethical and political problem is that the authority of mastery can then operate under the appearance of impersonal knowledge.

Boucher's distinctive contribution is to connect Lacanian discourse theory with speech act theory. He maps John Searle's categories of declarative and assertive speech acts onto the master's and university discourses. From this he develops the concept of the "bureaucratic speech act": an assertive pseudo-declaration that presents a normative or political decision as though it were merely the neutral statement of facts or expert necessity. Bureaucratic speech thus colonizes normative space by concealing command inside knowledge.

His final historical thesis concerns "reflexive modernity." Once university discourse becomes hegemonic, mastery does not disappear. It returns in privatized and charismatic form, while public discourse increasingly speaks the language of expertise, management, inclusion, evaluation, and modernization. The result is an articulation of university and master discourses that helps explain both the decline of symbolic efficiency and the peculiar authority of contemporary political leaders.

[Source: printed pp. 274-275 / PDF pp. 283-284]

## 2. Argument structure

### 2.1 Lacan's theory of modernity: from master to bureaucrat

Boucher begins by presenting Lacan's diagnosis of modernity as a displacement of the master by the bureaucrat, including the possibility that totalitarian leadership is a bureaucratic phenomenon rather than a return to traditional mastery. The underlying social problem is the expansion of rationalized knowledge and the apparent replacement of the mastery of persons by the administration of things.

This is not, however, a story of inevitable decline or liberation. Boucher stresses that Lacan does not offer a linear passage from master's discourse to analyst's discourse. Rotation among discourse positions is contingent. The four discourses form a structural repertoire in which particular configurations can become hegemonic without abolishing the others.

The university discourse is nevertheless central to modernity. It is connected to an ethical impasse in which traditional mastery and honor no longer supply a viable answer, while utilitarianism and fundamentalism form an unsatisfactory modern binary. Psychoanalytic discourse represents an ethical alternative, but Lacan does not convert this into a program of social revolution. Boucher recalls Lacan's judgment that the radical students of 1968, in their hysterical protest, were demanding a new master.

[Source: printed pp. 274-275 / PDF pp. 283-284]

### 2.2 Master's discourse, politics, and hysterical revolt

Boucher characterizes master's discourse as the discourse of self-identity and control. S1 occupies the dominant place and organizes S2, the field of knowledge, in conformity with the values of the master signifier. The divided subject is repressed beneath S1, while objet a appears as by-product.

The paradigm is the master-slave dialectic. The slave who gives way in the struggle is set to work and produces knowledge for the master. At the same time, the slave produces a universality and an alienated subjectivity that the master's discourse cannot fully recognize. This excluded or surplus dimension can return as hysterical revolt.

For Boucher, mastery is therefore inherently political and dialogical. It draws boundaries between inclusion and exclusion, friend and enemy, and is tied to governance. The master also founds new social links. Hysterical rebellion is mastery's immanent reverse rather than an automatic exit from it. A revolution can rotate positions without abolishing the structure of mastery, which is why Lacan distinguishes subversion from the hysterical demand for another master.

[Source: printed pp. 275-276 / PDF pp. 284-285]

### 2.3 Derrida, inaugural declarations, and the problem of authority

Boucher next compares Lacan with Derrida's account of speech acts. Derrida emphasizes iterability and the instability of performatives: inaugural declarations must rely on conventions that precede the new order they claim to found. Declarations of independence and constitutions are therefore structurally paradoxical.

Boucher agrees that inaugural speech acts contain an impossibility, but he criticizes Derrida for treating locution independently of illocutionary authority. Lacan, he argues, offers a psychoanalytic account of the contradiction. The performative inconsistency of an inaugural declaration is not simply a linguistic defect. It has the structure of master's discourse.

The declaration creates an order through a master signifier while generating a remainder. The new order promises a social harmony that it cannot deliver, so utopian fantasy emerges as by-product. The excluded demand can then return in hysterical revolt. Stabilizing the new order requires a supplementary system of knowledge that mobilizes rather than simply represses the fantasy. This opens the historical path from mastery to university discourse.

[Source: printed pp. 276-277 / PDF pp. 285-286]

### 2.4 University discourse as interpellation and legitimation

From the medieval university onward, Boucher argues, mastery increasingly depends on apparently disinterested knowledge that legitimates existing power. In university discourse, systematic knowledge occupies the dominant position and addresses subjects as material to be formed by education and administration.

Boucher treats university discourse as a discourse of interpellation. It does not merely describe a preexisting social world. By classifying, educating, diagnosing, evaluating, and administering, it helps produce the social relations and subjects that its knowledge purports to describe.

The university discourse can therefore be both a cover for master authority and an increasingly autonomous mode of domination. Its power lies precisely in the appearance that knowledge, rather than command, is speaking.

[Source: printed p. 277 / PDF p. 286]

### 2.5 Foucault, disciplinary knowledge, and the missing unconscious

Boucher uses Foucault's *Discipline and Punish* as a powerful analysis of the university discourse. Institutional knowledge disposes bodies and produces obedient subjects while presenting itself as neutral. Discipline forms the "soul" that internalizes social norms, and expert discourse hides the power invested in those norms.

He extracts several claims from Foucault: modern power works through impersonal disciplines; knowledge and power are inseparable; normalization substitutes for spectacular command; and subjects are formed within institutional techniques rather than merely repressed from outside.

Boucher's criticism is Lacanian. Foucault does not adequately account for the symbolic fiction and unconscious structure that make disciplinary arrangements effective. The Panopticon works not simply because a body is visibly coerced but because a symbolic possibility of being seen is internalized. Boucher argues that university discourse sutures the divided subject and excludes unconscious division from knowledge. Foucault describes the operation but, in Boucher's view, reproduces the exclusion of the unconscious that helps the operation work.

[Source: printed pp. 277-279 / PDF pp. 286-288]

### 2.6 Speech acts: locution, illocution, and perlocution

Boucher then turns to J. L. Austin and speech act theory because Lacan's discourses are simultaneously forms of speech and social bonds. The performative dimension of an utterance can institute the relation to which it refers.

He recalls the distinction between constative and performative utterances. A constative describes a state of affairs and can be judged true or false. A performative changes a social status through its enunciation. "I do" in a marriage ceremony does not merely report a marriage; under appropriate conditions it performs one.

Austin eventually replaces the binary with a threefold distinction: locutionary content, illocutionary force, and perlocutionary consequences. Every speech act contains both content and a force that establishes a relation between speaker and hearer. Perlocution names consequences such as persuasion, shock, or other effects that exceed the conventional act.

For Boucher, this excess requires a third term beyond speaker and hearer. The uptake of an utterance is mediated by the Other, which supplies and tests the institutional conditions under which the utterance can count as authoritative. This is the point at which speech act theory can be mapped onto Lacan's discourse matrices.

[Source: printed pp. 279-281 / PDF pp. 288-290]

### 2.7 Searle's conditions and Lacan's four positions

John Searle formalizes the conditions of satisfaction for different illocutionary forces. Boucher highlights four components of a speech act:

1. the illocutionary force or essential condition;
2. the propositional statement and its direction of fit between words and world;
3. the sincerity condition, or psychological state expressed by the act;
4. the conditions of satisfaction, including institutional positioning required for legitimacy.

Boucher proposes that these four components can be mapped onto Lacan's four positions. This is an interpretive construction of his own, not a formula from Seminar XVII.

[Source: printed pp. 280-282 / PDF pp. 289-291]

### 2.8 Declaratives as master's discourse

For declarative speech acts, the speaker institutes a relation by virtue of an authorized convention. The source prints Searle's declarative formula using `D`, a two-way world/word direction-of-fit symbol, a null sincerity symbol, and `(p)` for propositional content. The formal glyphs were visually checked on PDF p. 291 because text extraction flattened them.

Boucher maps the four components as follows:

```text
AGENT: S1  ->  OTHER: S2

D               (p)
illocutionary    propositional statement
force            and preparatory conditions

TRUTH: $         PRODUCT: a

null sincerity   conditions of satisfaction /
condition        direction-of-fit effect
```

The illocutionary force indicator functions as S1 because it governs the enunciation while not forming part of the semantic content of the proposition. The statement `(p)` is S2, the chain of knowledge addressed by the force of the declaration. The null sincerity condition corresponds to the divided subject, since the declarative's authorized performance need not express a full personal interiority. The resulting institutionalized state of affairs occupies the product position associated with objet a.

Boucher labels this the Lacanian analysis of declaratives as master's discourse.

[Source: printed pp. 282-283 / PDF pp. 291-292; diagram visually verified]

### 2.9 Assertives as university discourse

Boucher applies the same method to assertives. An assertion presents a proposition as corresponding to the world. Its agency is the chain of knowledge, while its truth claim is structurally subordinate to that chain.

The diagram on printed p. 284 / PDF p. 293 was visually checked because extraction damaged the layout. Boucher maps assertives as:

```text
AGENT: S2  ->  OTHER: a

(p)             downward direction of fit
proposition     words must conform to world

TRUTH: S1       PRODUCT: $

truth-value     belief / sincerity condition
indicator
```

This is his Lacanian analysis of assertives as university discourse. The proposition or chain of knowledge occupies the agent position. The truth-value indicator is placed beneath it as S1. The interlocutor receives the assertion as an object to be verified, while the belief or sincerity condition appears as the divided subject produced by the discourse.

[Source: printed p. 284 / PDF p. 293; diagram visually verified]

### 2.10 Che vuoi?, perlocution, and objet a

Boucher then defends his identification of the sincerity condition with the divided subject and of the conditions of satisfaction with objet a. Searle's Intentionality is not, on Boucher's reading, a simple conscious intention. It is linguistically expressed and can persist even when the speaker is personally insincere.

The hearer nonetheless retroactively imputes an intention to the speaker. This creates a gap between linguistic Intentionality and the psychological intention attributed to the agent. Every speech act can therefore provoke the question: what does the speaker really want, *Che vuoi?*

Boucher identifies the excess opened by this temporal gap with the field of perlocution and, through Shoshana Felman, with a referential excess in which the real leaves a trace in meaning. This excess is what allows him to connect perlocution to objet a and to the pleasure and power of performative speech.

[Source: printed pp. 284-285 / PDF pp. 293-294]

### 2.11 Bureaucratic speech acts as assertive pseudo-declarations

The decisive step comes when Boucher identifies the characteristic utterances of bureaucracy. Bureaucrats do not primarily issue naked commands. They produce judgments, evaluations, assessments, recommendations, and summaries. These are a special kind of declarative that takes the form of assertion.

Boucher calls them assertive pseudo-declarations. They have the political and institutional force of declarations but appear formally as neutral descriptions. In discourse terms, university discourse usurps the content of master's discourse while retaining its own form. Normative command is hidden inside apparently factual knowledge.

This is what Boucher calls the bureaucratic colonization of normative space. Modernity can be described as university discourse gradually subordinating traditional mastery. Reflexive modernity begins when this process has become hegemonic enough that university discourse turns back upon modern institutions themselves, multiplying expert systems, provisional rules, guidelines, and mechanisms of evaluation.

[Source: printed pp. 285-286 / PDF pp. 294-295]

### 2.12 Reflexive modernity, expert systems, and control

Boucher connects his Lacanian model with theories of reflexive modernization associated with Ulrich Beck and Anthony Giddens. In reflexive modernity, the certainties of modern institutions themselves become objects of expert scrutiny and revision.

The social result is not emancipation from power but fragmentation into multiple regulated domains. Disciplinary society gives way to a society of control in which guidance is ubiquitous, mobile, and commodified. Traditional big-Other guarantees weaken, but responsibility is transferred to committees, experts, protocols, and local substitutes for the absent big Other.

This intensifies anxiety because the subject is surrounded by systems that promise guidance while no single symbolic authority can close the field.

[Source: printed pp. 285-287 / PDF pp. 294-296]

### 2.13 New Labour as an example of bureaucratic political language

Boucher uses Tony Blair's New Labour and Norman Fairclough's linguistic analysis as an empirical example. Third Way political discourse relies heavily on lists of apparently complementary terms, managerial language, inclusion, modernization, and categorical assertions.

Its grammar is especially important. Passive constructions and nominalized processes remove identifiable agents from political decisions. Policies appear as objective necessities or neutral descriptions of what modernization requires. The language becomes managerial and promotional rather than openly political and dialogical.

At the same time, assertions about the knowledge economy, social inclusion, and modernization have the force of government declarations. The speech act therefore says, in effect, that this is simply how the world is while simultaneously instituting the policy it describes. This is Boucher's paradigmatic bureaucratic speech act.

The discourse of inclusion also produces an excluded remainder. The British people can be addressed as an object of management, while marginality is recoded as moral failure and criminalized. Inclusion therefore has a product: subjects are trained to distinguish productive citizenship from a pathologized or criminalized underclass.

[Source: printed pp. 287-288 / PDF pp. 296-297]

### 2.14 Decline of symbolic efficiency and the return of privatized mastery

Boucher closes by relating bureaucratic hegemony to the Lacanian thesis of declining symbolic efficiency. The weakening of paternal authority and the growth of therapeutic and bureaucratic regulation fragment the symbolic order into multiple local rules and language games.

The characteristic subject is described through the figure of pathological narcissism, externally related to norms and encouraged to treat them as manipulable guidelines. The superegoic command to enjoy replaces straightforward internalization of a single universal law.

Yet mastery does not vanish. Precisely because public authority justifies itself through expert knowledge, personal mastery returns through image, charisma, and private identification. Contemporary politicians claim to follow neutral evidence while cultivating a personal aura that gives their words performative force.

Boucher describes this as the reflexive return of the master as an uncanny double. Public normative space is bureaucratized, while the authority that bureaucracy disavows reappears as privatized charisma. Bureaucratic speech acts are the linguistic form through which this articulation of hegemonic university discourse and subordinated master discourse is legitimated.

[Source: printed pp. 288-290 / PDF pp. 297-299]

## 3. Key Lacanian concepts

### Master's discourse

Boucher emphasizes S1 as authoritative illocutionary force, S2 as the knowledge ordered by command, the divided subject as repressed truth, and objet a as the surplus or fantasmatic product. Politics and founding declarations are paradigmatic forms.

### University discourse

University discourse is the dominant form of bureaucratic and expert modernity. Knowledge speaks as agent, concealing the master signifier that authorizes it and producing divided subjects through apparently neutral administration.

### Hysteric's discourse

Hysterical revolt is mastery's immanent reverse. It questions the master but can remain a demand for another master. Boucher therefore distinguishes revolt from structural subversion.

### Objet a and perlocutionary excess

Boucher connects objet a to the excess generated when a speech act does more than its conventional illocution specifies. The hearer's question about what the speaker really wants opens a gap in which perlocution and unconscious desire appear.

### S1 and speech-act authority

The illocutionary force indicator is mapped to S1 because it authorizes and organizes an utterance without belonging to its propositional semantic content.

### S2 and bureaucratic knowledge

Propositional chains, expertise, assessments, and procedural descriptions occupy the position of S2. When S2 speaks as agent, normative command can appear as merely factual necessity.

### Decline of symbolic efficiency

Boucher uses this later Lacanian orientation to describe a fragmented social order in which rules proliferate without a single trusted universal law. Bureaucratic control and personal charisma grow together rather than excluding one another.

## 4. Relation to Seminar XVII

Boucher takes Seminar XVII's four-discourse matrix as the foundation of a social theory of modernity. The seminar supplies the distinction between master's and university discourses, the relation between 1968 protest and hysterical demand, and the concept of discourse as social link.

His mapping of speech act theory onto the four discourse positions is an original extension. Lacan does not in Seminar XVII identify Searle's declaratives with master's discourse or assertives with university discourse. Nor does Lacan coin Boucher's category of the bureaucratic speech act.

The historical theory of reflexive modernity is likewise Boucher's synthesis of Lacan with Foucault, Derrida, Austin, Searle, Felman, Beck, Giddens, Zizek, and Fairclough. The value of the essay lies precisely in this extension, but the corpus should retain the distinction between Lacan's formal apparatus and Boucher's political-linguistic application.

## 5. Examples, interlocutors and external references

Boucher engages Derrida on performativity and declarations, Foucault on disciplinary knowledge, Austin and Searle on speech acts, Shoshana Felman on performative failure, and Beck and Giddens on reflexive modernization. Zizek appears in the account of declining symbolic efficiency and substitute small big Others.

Tony Blair and New Labour provide the main political example. Fairclough's linguistic analysis supplies evidence for passive grammar, nominalized processes, managerial language, inclusion rhetoric, categorical assertions, and the knowledge-economy vocabulary that Boucher identifies as bureaucratic speech acts.

## 6. Mathemes, formulas, figures and diagrams

### Declaratives mapped onto master's discourse

The source diagram on printed p. 283 / PDF p. 292 was visually verified.

```text
AGENT: S1  ->  OTHER: S2

D               (p)
illocutionary    statement / propositional content
force

TRUTH: $         PRODUCT: a

null sincerity   conditions of satisfaction /
condition        instituted relation
```

Boucher identifies this as a Lacanian analysis of declaratives as master's discourse.

### Assertives mapped onto university discourse

The source diagram on printed p. 284 / PDF p. 293 was visually verified.

```text
AGENT: S2  ->  OTHER: a

(p)             direction of fit:
proposition     words conform to world

TRUTH: S1       PRODUCT: $

truth-value     belief / sincerity condition
indicator
```

Boucher identifies this as a Lacanian analysis of assertives as university discourse.

### Note on Searle notation

The source also prints compact Searlean formulas for declaratives and assertives using specialized direction-of-fit, truth-value, and null-sincerity glyphs. Because those glyphs are easily corrupted in text extraction, the reconstruction preserves their functional meaning and the visually verified Lacanian matrices rather than substituting uncertain Unicode approximations.

## 7. Interpretive contribution and limits

Boucher's most distinctive contribution is the category of bureaucratic speech acts. A bureaucratic utterance is politically performative while disguising its performativity as neutral description. It therefore captures how university discourse can usurp the normative function of mastery without speaking in the old master's voice.

A second contribution is his non-teleological theory of modernity. The university discourse can become hegemonic without eliminating master's discourse. Mastery is subordinated, privatized, and rearticulated, then returns through charisma and image beneath the public language of expertise.

A third contribution is the speech-act mapping itself. It provides a technical bridge between Lacan's discourse theory and linguistic pragmatics. It should be treated as Boucher's model, not as an established equivalence explicitly asserted by Lacan.

Finally, the New Labour case shows how the model is meant to be used empirically. Grammar, institutional authority, and policy discourse can combine so that assertions have declarative force while refusing to acknowledge their political agency. This is Boucher's explanation for the bureaucratic colonization of normative space.

## 8. Retrieval anchors
